scenarios.title: The Service That Won't Start
scenarios.situation: A line-of-business app stops working on a Windows Server. You open Services (services.msc) and find its service in a Stopped state; its Startup Type is Automatic. A colleague says to just click Start and move on.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first response, and what do you check after?
choices: Start the service, then immediately check the Event Logs (System and Application) for the errors that stopped it — restarting without a cause lets it fail again.
Reinstall the application; a stopped service always means a corrupt install.
Set the startup type to Manual so it cannot crash again.
Reboot the server immediately without checking anything.
scenarios.why: Services with Automatic startup do not stop themselves — something told the service to stop. Event Viewer (System log for service-control events, Application log for the app's own errors) is the causal layer; services.msc is only the control layer. The professional habit is control first, cause second, fix third.
scenarios.hint: Which two windows show you what the service did (control) versus why it did it (cause)?
objectives: Windows core administration: services and event logs

scenarios.title: NTFS vs Share Permissions
scenarios.situation: A user complains they cannot write to a shared folder, though their manager swears 'everyone has full control on the share.' You inspect the folder and see NTFS permissions grant the user's group Read-only.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the user blocked, and what is the right fix?
choices: Windows applies the most restrictive of the combined share and NTFS permissions — NTFS Read-only wins. Grant Write in the NTFS permissions (following least privilege) rather than opening the share further.
Share permissions override NTFS, so the user should already have access — the problem must be the network.
Give the user Full Control at both layers to eliminate all future tickets.
Delete the share and recreate it; permissions do not survive a share rebuild.
scenarios.why: Effective access is the intersection of share and NTFS permissions: the most restrictive permission always wins. The modern best practice is to set the share to broad access (e.g., Authenticated Users: Full Control) and enforce the real policy at the NTFS layer, where permissions are granular, inheritable, and auditable.
scenarios.hint: When two layers both say something, which one wins — the generous one or the strict one?
objectives: Windows core administration: NTFS and sharing

scenarios.title: The Locked-Out Finance User
scenarios.situation: A finance user cannot log in and the help desk unlocked their account twice today. You check Active Directory Users and Computers and see the account is in the Finance OU, which has a Group Policy requiring a 15-character password, while the user keeps setting a 10-character one.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the proper resolution?
choices: A Group Policy on the Finance OU enforces 15-character passwords; the user's 10-character password fails policy, so logons fail. Reset the password to a policy-compliant value and explain the requirement.
The user is being hacked; disable the account immediately.
Move the user to a different OU to escape the policy.
Group Policy is broken and should be unlinked from the Finance OU.
scenarios.why: Group Policy applies by OU: policies linked to the Finance OU win for accounts in that OU (the LSDOU order — Local, Site, Domain, OU — means the closest link wins on conflict). The unlocks treated the symptom; the password-policy mismatch was the cause. The fix is a compliant password plus user education — not moving the user or breaking policy for one person.
scenarios.hint: If a setting lives on the OU and the user lives in the OU, where do you look first — the user or the policy?
objectives: Active Directory: OUs and Group Policy

scenarios.title: PowerShell: The Pipeline Fix
scenarios.situation: You need a list of all services currently running on a server whose names start with 'SQL', and you want just their names and statuses on screen. You know Get-Service lists services and Where-Object filters them.
choices: Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' -and $_.Name -like 'SQL*' } | Select-Object Name, Status
Get-Service -Name 'SQL*' | Where-Object Status = Running
Where-Object { Name -like 'SQL*' } | Get-Service -Running
Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10
scenarios.why: The pipeline passes objects, not text: Get-Service emits service objects, Where-Object filters on their Status and Name properties ($_.Status, $_.Name), and Select-Object projects just the properties you want. The -like operator with a wildcard handles the 'starts with SQL' match. Memorizing the cmdlet names matters less than the pattern: get → filter → shape.
scenarios.hint: What does the pipeline carry between commands — text lines or objects with properties?

scenarios.title: DNS: The Intranet Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that 'intranet' resolves to an old IP on some workstations but the correct new IP on others. The DNS zone on the Windows DNS server was updated an hour ago. You confirm the server returns the new address.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm it on a broken workstation?
choices: Stale resolver cache or an outdated DHCP-provided DNS configuration on the affected workstations. Run ipconfig /displaydns to inspect the cache and ipconfig /flushdns plus ipconfig /registerdns to refresh it.
The DNS server is lying; rebuild the zone from scratch.
The workstations need new network cards.
Block port 53 at the firewall to force a different resolution path.
scenarios.why: Windows caches DNS answers locally, and clients keep using the cache until its TTL expires — so a zone change propagates unevenly. ipconfig /displaydns shows the cached entry, /flushdns clears it, and /registerdns re-registers the client. When 'some machines work and some don't' after a DNS change, the cache is suspect number one.
scenarios.hint: If the server is right but the client is wrong, where between them can an old answer hide?

scenarios.title: Kerberos vs NTLM at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: After a domain migration, a legacy application authenticates users but its audit logs show NTLM authentication instead of Kerberos. The app runs on a server joined to the new domain, and users authenticate fine — but security policy requires Kerberos everywhere it is supported.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely reason the app fell back to NTLM?
choices: The application or its service principal name (SPN) is misconfigured — Kerberos needs a valid SPN for the service, and without one (or with a duplicate SPN), Windows silently falls back to NTLM. Check SPN registration with setspn -L and the event logs for Kerberos errors.
NTLM is stronger than Kerberos, so this is an improvement.
Kerberos requires the firewall to be disabled.
The domain controllers need to be rebooted nightly for Kerberos to work.
scenarios.why: Kerberos authentication requires the client to find a ticket for the exact service principal name; a missing or duplicated SPN breaks ticket issuance and Windows degrades to NTLM without telling the user. This is why legacy apps 'work but show NTLM' after migrations: the app was never registered properly in the new domain. setspn -L <account> lists registered SPNs; duplicates are a classic migration artifact.
scenarios.hint: Kerberos answers the question 'who vouches for this service?' What record provides that answer?
objectives: Active Directory: Kerberos and NTLM authentication

scenarios.title: The service that starts manually but not at boot
scenarios.situation: The backup agent service runs fine when started by hand, but every Monday it is stopped after the weekend reboot. Startup type: Automatic. Event log shows 7000 (timeout) then 7009 at boot.
evidence: Backup agent: Automatic, depends on nothing declared. Needs the backup NAS mounted (network + storage).
Service starts before the network storage is ready — 30s timeout, fails. Manual start later works (storage ready by then).
choices: Missing service dependency: the agent needs the network/storage stack ready first. Fix: set the service to Automatic (Delayed Start) and/or declare dependencies (DependOnService) so it starts after the required stack. The 7000/7009 timeouts at boot with manual-start success is the signature of a boot-ordering problem, not a broken service
The service is corrupt; reinstall it
Set it to Manual and have someone start it Mondays
The server needs faster disks so boot completes sooner
scenarios.why: Services start in dependency order at boot — a service that needs network storage but declares no dependency races the storage stack and loses, timing out at 30 seconds (7009). Manual starts work because the race is over. Reinstalling does not add the missing dependency. Manual Mondays institutionalize the failure. Faster disks might win the race sometimes — 'sometimes' is not a fix. The correct tools: Automatic (Delayed Start) for services that can wait ~2 minutes, or explicit DependOnService for hard requirements. The diagnostic pattern to remember: 'works manually, fails at boot' = boot ordering (dependencies, delayed start, or a dependency service that itself is delayed). Check the Dependencies tab before anything else.
scenarios.hint: What does 'works manually, fails at boot' indicate?

scenarios.title: The registry edit with no backup
scenarios.situation: An admin 'tweaked' HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer for a performance tip from a blog. The server no longer boots to network — no shares, no RDP. No registry backup was taken. Last Known Good does not help (it booted 'successfully' several times since).
scenarios.prompt: What are the recovery options, in order?
evidence: Boots, but network stack broken. Change: registry edit, no export. Several successful boots since (Last Known Good overwritten).
System State backup from Sunday (2 days ago), WinRE boot media, no documented original value.
choices: Ordered recovery: (1) if you know the exact key, fix it via WinRE offline registry edit (load the hive, correct the value); (2) System State restore from Sunday (loses 2 days of changes — acceptable vs. a dead server); (3) rebuild as last resort. Going forward: export before EVERY edit (reg export takes 5 seconds), prefer GPO Preferences over raw edits, and never apply blog 'tweaks' to production without a lab test
Reinstall Windows; the registry is unfixable
Keep trying random registry values until it works
The blog tip was wrong; comment on the blog
scenarios.why: The registry is editable offline: WinRE + regedit can load the broken hive and fix the known key — IF you know what was changed (another reason to document edits). System State restore is the reliable fallback (2 days of churn is the price of no export). Reinstalling for one bad value is surrender. Random edits compound the damage. The real lesson is the 5-second habit: reg export HKLM\... backup.reg BEFORE the edit, and the restore is one double-click. Production registry edits also deserve a change ticket and a lab test — 'a blog said so' is not a change rationale. The registry has no undo; the export IS the undo. Make it muscle memory.
scenarios.hint: What is the 'undo' for a registry edit?

scenarios.title: The 5-command triage
scenarios.situation: A junior admin pages you: 'The app server is down!' You have 60 seconds before the bridge call. You need the fastest possible signal on what is actually wrong.
evidence: App server unreachable per monitoring. No info yet on scope.
In 60 seconds, determine: is it the server, the network, or the app?
choices: Bottom-up, fastest signal first: (1) Test-NetConnection -ComputerName srv -Port 3389 (or ping) — is the HOST reachable? (2) Enter-PSSession / Invoke-Command { Get-Service } — is the OS alive and manageable? (3) Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 20 — what just happened (reboot? service crash? disk error?)? (4) Get-Counter or Task Manager equivalent — resource exhaustion? (5) app-specific check (port, service, log). The ORDER matters: each step rules out a layer before you spend time on the next
RDP in and look around
Restart the server; it fixes most things
Call the app vendor immediately
scenarios.why: Triage is layered elimination under time pressure: host reachability first (if ping fails, it is network/power — stop investigating the app), then OS manageability (remoting works = OS alive), then recent events (the log usually names the failure: unexpected shutdown 6008, service 7034, disk errors), then resources, then the app. RDP-and-look is slow and interactive (and RDP may be the broken thing). Rebooting before diagnosis destroys evidence and may not fix anything (and causes an outage if it was just the app). The vendor cannot help before you know the layer. Sixty seconds of ordered triage beats twenty minutes of random clicking — and the bridge call goes from 'it is down' to 'host is up, OS responsive, the app service crashed at 14:02 with event 7034, restarting it now.' That is the difference triage makes.
scenarios.hint: Why does triage order matter under time pressure?

scenarios.title: The Windows Systems Administration Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Windows Systems Administration is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Windows Systems Administration?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Windows Systems Administration issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Windows Systems Administration is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Windows Systems Administration supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Windows Systems Administration failure in Windows Admin.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Windows Systems Administration
evidence: All Windows Systems Administration components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The page file on C:
scenarios.situation: A SQL server's page file is system-managed on C: (100GB SSD, 85% full). Under load, paging competes with the OS and SQL binaries for the same spindles. The admin asks if the page file should be disabled ('we have 128GB RAM').
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct page-file guidance?
evidence: 128GB RAM, page file system-managed on C:, C: at 85%. SQL Server with locked pages.
Occasional severe slowdowns correlating with C: latency spikes.
choices: Right-size and relocate, do not disable: keep a page file (Windows expects one — crash dumps and commit accounting need it), move it OFF the OS volume to dedicated fast storage, and size it sanely (for 128GB RAM with SQL locked pages, a modest fixed size, not system-managed unbounded). Disabling risks commit-limit failures and loses crash dumps; the problem is placement and contention, not existence
Disable the page file; 128GB RAM is plenty
Let Windows manage it; defaults are fine
Add more RAM to avoid paging entirely
scenarios.why: The page file serves three masters: virtual-memory backing, commit-limit accounting, and crash-dump capture. Disabling it removes all three — applications can hit commit-limit failures even with free RAM (commit charge vs physical RAM are different accountings), and the next BSOD produces no dump for diagnosis. System-managed on a nearly-full OS volume is the worst placement: paging I/O fights the OS and binaries on the same spindles, and growth threatens the boot volume. More RAM does not change the accounting or dump requirements. The correct posture: a fixed-size page file on dedicated fast storage (separate from OS and data), sized for dump needs + headroom, monitored. Page-file design is a small decision with outsized consequences — make it deliberately.
scenarios.hint: Why should you not disable the page file even with abundant RAM?

scenarios.title: The CPU that is busy doing nothing
scenarios.situation: Task Manager shows 30% CPU in use, but the server crawls. Resource Monitor reveals the 30% is almost entirely 'Hardware Interrupts' (DPCs) — a faulty NIC driver is interrupt-storming.
scenarios.prompt: What does high interrupt CPU indicate?
evidence: Processor(_Total)\% Interrupt Time ~28%, DPC Time elevated. Process CPU low.
New NIC driver deployed last week; slowness started then.
choices: Driver/hardware problem, not workload: interrupt/DPC time is CPU spent in kernel servicing hardware — 28% means the hardware (via its driver) is screaming for attention. The new NIC driver is the prime suspect (timing matches). Fix: roll back or update the driver, check firmware, and if needed replace the NIC. No amount of app tuning fixes interrupt storms — this is below the OS's process layer
The CPU is too slow; upgrade it
A process is hiding its CPU usage; find it
Reboot weekly to clear the interrupts
scenarios.why: CPU time splits into process time (your code) and interrupt/DPC time (kernel servicing hardware). High interrupt time with low process time means the machine is busy servicing HARDWARE, not running YOUR workload — Task Manager's headline number conflates the two. No process will show the usage because no process owns it; the driver does. A faster CPU just services interrupts faster (the storm continues). Weekly reboots reset the symptom until the driver storms again. The diagnosis is in the counter: % Interrupt Time + % DPC Time elevated = look at drivers/firmware/hardware, starting with what changed recently (last week's NIC driver). This is why admins read the DETAILED counters, not the headline number — the headline lies by aggregation.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between process CPU time and interrupt time?

scenarios.title: Monday morning: nobody can log on
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:55 AM: helpdesk flooded — nobody can log on across all three sites. Friday's change: the networking team 'optimized' DNS, pointing all clients at the new ISP DNS resolvers instead of the domain controllers. Servers were not changed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
evidence: Friday 17:30: DHCP scope option 006 changed from DC IPs to ISP DNS (8.8.8.8-style). No other changes.
Clients resolve internet fine; nslookup for _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.local fails. Cached logons work for previously-logged-on laptops.
choices: DNS misconfiguration: clients must use AD-integrated DNS (the DCs) to locate domain services via SRV records — ISP resolvers know nothing about the internal _msdcs zone. Fix: revert DHCP option 006 to the DCs immediately; previously-logged-on machines work only because of cached credentials, which will expire
The domain controllers are down; reboot them
The ISP DNS is blocking AD traffic; call the ISP
Passwords expired en masse over the weekend; reset them
scenarios.why: This is the canonical 'AD is down but AD is fine' incident: Active Directory's service location is DNS SRV records in the _msdcs zone, which exist only on the domain's DNS servers. Point clients at external resolvers and those records vanish — logon, GPO, and DFS all break simultaneously while 'the internet works.' Cached logons mask it for machines with recent logons, which is why some laptops still work. Rebooting healthy DCs, blaming the ISP, or resetting passwords all miss the layer: name resolution. The fix is one DHCP option change plus ipconfig /renew, and the lesson is permanent — DNS is always step one in AD troubleshooting.
scenarios.hint: Which DNS records do domain clients need, and where do they live?

scenarios.title: The PDC emulator is gone
scenarios.situation: The VM hosting the PDC emulator role was accidentally deleted Friday night. Monday: password changes fail ('the system cannot contact a domain controller'), time is drifting on clients, and GPO edits warn about the PDC.
evidence: PDC emulator holder deleted; VHDX unrecoverable. Other DCs healthy. netdom query fsmo shows the PDC role with no reachable owner.
Password changes, time sync hierarchy, and GPO default editing all target the PDC — all degraded.
choices: Seize the PDC emulator role to a healthy DC (ntdsutil / PowerShell), verify time sync and password changes recover, clean up the deleted DC's metadata, and NEVER bring the deleted VM back — then review why a role holder had no backup and why deletion was possible
Restore the deleted VM from backup; it will resume the role
Transfer the role gracefully from the deleted DC
Wait — the role will auto-migrate to another DC
scenarios.why: A deleted role holder cannot transfer (transfer needs the live owner) and roles never auto-migrate — seizure is the designed path for dead holders. Restoring the deleted VM risks USN rollback and a resurrected DC with stale state; the correct sequence is seize-then-metadata-cleanup, treating the old DC as permanently gone. Password changes fail because they are forwarded to the PDC; time drifts because the domain time hierarchy roots at the PDC; GPO tools default to editing on the PDC. All three symptoms point at one role, which is the diagnostic lesson: know what each FSMO role does and its blast radius. Then fix the process gaps (backups, deletion protection) that allowed it.
scenarios.hint: Transfer vs seize: when is each correct, and what must never return after a seize?

scenarios.title: The org-chart OU disaster
scenarios.situation: The previous admin built OUs mirroring the org chart: Sales, Marketing, Engineering, each with sub-OUs per manager. Reorgs happen twice a year. Every reorg breaks GPO targeting, delegation has to be redone, and the helpdesk cannot find computers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct OU design principle?
evidence: OU=Sales > OU=TeamA > OU=SmithsTeam — 47 OUs, rebuilt twice yearly. GPOs linked per manager-OU.
Each reorg: computers move, GPO links break, delegation re-done, weeks of tickets.
choices: Design OUs by administration need, not org chart: Workstations, Servers, Service Accounts, plus location-based OUs if policy differs by site. People move between managers constantly; machines' management needs barely change. GPOs link to stable admin OUs; group membership (not OU placement) handles the fluid people stuff
Automate the OU rebuilds with a script after each reorg
Flatten everything to one OU and use security filtering for all GPOs
Mirror the new org chart more carefully this time
scenarios.why: Org charts are the most volatile structure in a company; building infrastructure on them guarantees perpetual rebuilds. Computers need policy by what they ARE (workstation, server, kiosk, site) — attributes that survive reorgs. Scripting the rebuild automates the toil without removing it. Flattening to one OU plus security filtering works technically but makes GPO management opaque (dozens of filtered GPOs on one container). And a 'better' org-chart mirror just fails more elegantly next reorg. The principle: OUs model stable administrative boundaries; security groups model fluid human relationships. Get this right once and reorgs become a group-membership task, not an infrastructure project.
scenarios.hint: What should OUs model — people or administration needs?

scenarios.title: The NTLM in the logs
scenarios.situation: Security review: 40% of authentication events are NTLM, not Kerberos. The web app team says 'it works, do not touch it.' The CISO wants Kerberos everywhere possible.
scenarios.prompt: What does NTLM prevalence indicate and how do you fix it?
evidence: NTLMv2 events for HTTP/webapp01 from hundreds of clients. setspn -Q HTTP/webapp01 shows NO SPN registered; the app pool runs as a domain service account.
Works, but: no mutual authentication, credential-theft exposure (relay), weaker auditing.
choices: Missing SPN: without HTTP/webapp01 registered to the service account, clients cannot get a Kerberos service ticket and silently fall back to NTLM. Fix: register the SPN to the correct account (setspn -S), verify no duplicates, and watch NTLM events drop. Then investigate remaining NTLM sources one by one — each is a misconfiguration with a fix
NTLM is normal; the CISO's goal is unrealistic
Disable NTLM via GPO immediately to force Kerberos
The app needs reinstalling to support Kerberos
scenarios.why: NTLM fallback is Kerberos failing quietly: the protocol tries Kerberos first and degrades when it cannot (missing/duplicate SPN, name mismatch, time skew). Here the cause is visible in one command — no SPN, so no service ticket is possible. 'It works' is the enemy: NTLM works while exposing the environment to relay attacks and pass-the-hash. Disabling NTLM before fixing the causes breaks the app (the fallback was load-bearing). Reinstalling is unnecessary — the app speaks Kerberos fine; the directory just lacks the mapping. The method generalizes: NTLM in logs is a symptom list; each entry has a fixable cause (usually SPN or name resolution). Drive it down systematically.
scenarios.hint: What does NTLM fallback tell you about Kerberos health?

scenarios.title: The helpdesk that could reset the CEO
scenarios.situation: Audit finds the helpdesk group has 'Reset Password' delegated at the DOMAIN root. They can reset any account — including Domain Admins and the CEO. The delegation was done 'to make the wizard simpler.'
evidence: Helpdesk group: reset-password + unlock at domain root. No scoping.
Any helpdesk account (or its compromise) = full account takeover of any user, then privilege escalation path.
choices: Re-scope delegation to the specific OUs containing regular user accounts (e.g., OU=Employees), explicitly excluding privileged OUs (Admins, Service Accounts) — least privilege: helpdesk resets passwords for the population they support, never for admins. Add auditing on privileged-OU modifications
Remove the delegation entirely; admins will handle all resets
It is fine — helpdesk staff are trusted employees
Move the CEO's account to a separate domain
scenarios.why: Delegation at the domain root grants the right over every object class-wide — including the accounts that administer the helpdesk staff themselves. That inverts the trust hierarchy: the lowest-privilege support tier can disable the highest-privilege accounts (reset + set 'must change password' = takeover). 'Trusted employees' confuses HR trust with security architecture — the threat is account compromise, not malice. Removing delegation entirely destroys helpdesk function. A separate domain for the CEO is architectural overkill for a scoping problem. The fix is boring and correct: delegate at the OU containing the supported population, carve out privileged OUs, and audit. Delegation should always be reviewed with 'who is the most privileged account this reaches?'
scenarios.hint: What is wrong with delegating at the domain root?

scenarios.title: The five-minute skew
scenarios.situation: Intermittent logon failures across the finance VLAN: some mornings users get 'the trust relationship' or Kerberos errors; afternoons are fine. The finance switch was replaced last month with a model that does not do NTP well. The PDC emulator is healthy.
evidence: Failures cluster in mornings, finance VLAN only. Affected machines show time 6–8 minutes behind the DCs.
New switch last month; finance VLAN clients point at the switch as NTP source via DHCP option 042.
choices: Time skew breaking Kerberos: the 5-minute tolerance is exceeded on finance clients each morning (drift overnight, worse when idle). Kerberos rejects the tickets — logon fails. Fix: point domain members at the domain time hierarchy (PDC emulator), not the switch; domain members should sync from DCs, period
The trust relationship is broken; rejoin the machines to the domain
The finance VLAN has a network issue; replace the switch again
Kerberos is flaky; enable NTLM fallback for finance
scenarios.why: Kerberos authenticators have a 5-minute freshness window — beyond it, tickets are rejected as potential replays. Six to eight minutes of skew is not 'close enough'; it is a hard failure, and mornings are worst because idle machines drift overnight. Rejoining the domain 'fixes' nothing (the trust is fine; time is not). The switch is not broken — it was just never a suitable time source. Enabling NTLM fallback treats the symptom by downgrading security. The rule is absolute for domain members: time comes from the domain hierarchy (PDC emulator at the root), via w32time defaults. Any DHCP option or GPO pointing clients elsewhere is a logon-failure generator. When logons fail intermittently with time patterns, check time before anything else.
scenarios.hint: Why does Kerberos care about clock skew?

scenarios.title: The deleted OU
scenarios.situation: A script bug deleted OU=Contractors (300 users, 40 groups) at 2 PM. The admin enabled the AD Recycle Bin last year 'just in case.' Users are locked out now.
evidence: OU deleted 30 minutes ago. AD Recycle Bin enabled (forest-wide). No backup newer than last night.
Restore the OU with all objects and group memberships, fast.
choices: Restore from the AD Recycle Bin: deleted objects are recoverable with attributes and memberships intact (Restore-ADObject / AD Administrative Center). It is the designed path for exactly this — minutes, not hours, and no backup needed. Then fix the script and add -WhatIf/scope guards
Restore last night's System State backup authoritatively
Recreate the 300 users manually from HR records
Wait — replication will restore the OU automatically
scenarios.why: The Recycle Bin exists for this exact scenario: deleted objects sit in the Deleted Objects container with most attributes preserved, restorable in minutes. Authoritative backup restore would roll back every change since last night across the domain — massive overkill that creates new problems. Manual recreation loses SIDs, passwords, and group memberships (access breaks subtly for weeks). Replication never un-deletes; it faithfully replicates the deletion everywhere. The meta-lesson: the admin's 'just in case' decision last year just saved the afternoon. Enable the Recycle Bin on day one of every forest — it is irreversible to enable and invaluable exactly once, which is enough.
scenarios.hint: What does the AD Recycle Bin preserve that manual recreation loses?

scenarios.title: The GPO that never applies
scenarios.situation: A new 'Disable USB storage' GPO is linked to OU=Workstations, but USB drives still work on test machines. gpresult /r shows the GPO under 'Denied GPOs' with reason 'Empty'.
scenarios.prompt: What does 'Empty' mean and what is the fix?
evidence: Computer Configuration: Removable Storage Access deny-write configured. User Configuration: not configured (empty). Link: OU=Workstations.
Denied GPOs: 'Disable USB storage' — Reason: Empty.
choices: 'Empty' means the GPO has no settings applicable to the processing side: the GPO contains only Computer settings, but something (security filtering, loopback state, or the GPO status) caused only the User side to evaluate — most commonly the GPO's status is set to 'User settings disabled' or filtering excludes computers. Check GPO Status (enable both sides), security filtering (computers need Read+Apply), and confirm the test machine is actually in OU=Workstations
Run gpupdate /force; it just needs a refresh
The USB policy does not work on Windows 11; use another method
Link the GPO at the domain root instead
scenarios.why: 'Denied — Empty' is gpresult telling you the GPO evaluated to nothing for that processing pass: no applicable settings on the side being processed. gpupdate /force re-processes the same empty evaluation — it cannot fix scope. The policy mechanism works fine on current Windows; the problem is targeting. Domain-root linking would 'work' by applying to everything including servers — the wrong fix. The checklist: GPO Status (both sides enabled?), link location (is the machine really in that OU — check the distinguished name), security filtering (does the computer object have Apply rights?), WMI filters (is one excluding it?). One of these is always the answer; gpresult's Denied section names it.
scenarios.hint: What does gpresult 'Denied — Empty' actually tell you?

scenarios.title: The version mismatch
scenarios.situation: A GPO edit on DC1 does not apply to clients using DC2. On DC1, GPMC shows version 12; on DC2, version 10. SYSVOL on DC2 lacks the newest policy files. repadmin shows replication healthy.
evidence: AD version (12) vs SYSVOL content (10) on DC2. AD replication healthy; SYSVOL (DFSR) not converging for the SYSVOL share.
Clients on DC2 get the old policy; no errors, just stale settings.
choices: SYSVOL replication (DFSR) is stalled while AD replication works — a GPO is TWO things (AD object with version + SYSVOL files with content) and they replicate independently. Diagnose DFSR (event log, backlog with dfsrdiag), fix the SYSVOL replication; the version mismatch resolves when content converges. Never 'fix' by editing on DC2 (forks the GPO)
AD replication is lying; reboot both DCs
Delete and recreate the GPO
Force clients to use DC1 via DNS changes
scenarios.why: A Group Policy Object is a split-brain design by nature: the AD object carries metadata and version, SYSVOL carries the actual settings files, and they replicate through different mechanisms (AD replication vs DFSR). Healthy repadmin with stale SYSVOL is the signature of DFSR trouble — check the DFS Replication event log and backlog. Rebooting healthy DCs is hope-based. Recreating the GPO loses history and does not fix DFSR (the new GPO's SYSVOL would stall too). Pinning clients to DC1 masks the fault until DC1 needs maintenance. The lesson: when a GPO 'does not apply,' check version on the client's DC in both AD and SYSVOL — the mismatch tells you which replication is broken.
scenarios.hint: Why can AD replication be healthy while a GPO is stale?

scenarios.title: The enforced mystery
scenarios.situation: A drive-mapping preference targets Finance users, but it also appears for IT admins logging into finance workstations. The admin GPO is linked at OU=Workstations with Enforced set 'to make sure it applies.' Block Inheritance is set on the Finance OU.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this design?
evidence: OU=Workstations: 'Lockdown' GPO, Enforced. OU=Finance (child): Block Inheritance + 'Finance Maps' GPO.
Enforced 'Lockdown' wins over Block Inheritance — by design. IT admins get finance restrictions on finance machines.
choices: Enforced beats Block Inheritance — always. The design fights itself: Block Inheritance on Finance is silently overridden by the Enforced parent link. Fix: remove Enforced (use it only for true non-negotiables), and handle the admin exception properly — security filtering, loopback, or a separate admin OU — instead of pitting Enforced against Block
Remove Block Inheritance from Finance
Enforced is broken; open a support case
Move the IT admins to a different domain
scenarios.why: Enforced and Block Inheritance are opposing forces and Enforced always wins — that is documented, not a bug. The design tried to have it both ways (inherit everything except when blocked, except the enforced stuff) and produced an unreadable precedence map. Removing Block Inheritance 'fixes' the symptom by surrendering the Finance OU's autonomy. The real fix is design discipline: Enforced is for the tiny set of truly non-overrideable settings (security baselines), used rarely enough that every instance is memorable. Exceptions for admins belong in targeting (security groups, loopback, separate OUs) — explicit and visible — not in precedence warfare. If your GPO design needs a diagram to explain, simplify it.
scenarios.hint: What beats what: Enforced vs Block Inheritance?

scenarios.title: The kiosk that was not locked down
scenarios.situation: Library kiosks should lock down ANY user who logs on. The lockdown GPO (user settings) is linked to OU=Kiosks (computer objects). Domain admins testing on kiosks get the full lockdown too — including the inability to open admin tools to fix the kiosks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct loopback design?
evidence: User-settings GPO linked to computer OU — without loopback, user settings follow the USER's OU, so the kiosk GPO's user settings never applied. Someone enabled loopback Replace; now it applies to everyone including admins.
Lockdown for normal users on kiosks; admins exempt for maintenance.
choices: Loopback Replace is correct for kiosks (user settings follow the computer), but the admin exemption is missing: use security filtering to DENY Apply to the admin group (or a separate admin account workflow), so Replace applies the kiosk user-settings to everyone EXCEPT admins. Alternatively Replace + dedicated local admin account for maintenance
Disable loopback; link the user settings to the users' OUs instead
Remove the lockdown; kiosks do not need it
Give admins a different kiosk
scenarios.why: Without loopback, user settings in a computer-OU GPO are inert — the kiosk was never actually locking down arbitrary users (the original bug). Loopback Replace fixes that by making the computer's user-settings win. But Replace is indiscriminate: it replaces for admins too, which bricks maintenance access. The complete design pairs Replace with an exemption — security-filter deny for the admin group is the standard pattern. Linking user settings to user OUs defeats the kiosk concept (any user anywhere gets locked down). Removing the lockdown abandons the requirement. The pattern to remember: kiosk = computer OU + loopback Replace + user settings + admin exemption via filtering. All four parts.
scenarios.hint: What are the four parts of a correct kiosk GPO design?

scenarios.title: The 20-minute logon
scenarios.situation: After a new GPO deploys a 400MB software package via startup script, all workstations take 20 minutes to boot. Users are furious. The GPO uses a synchronous startup script.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the better deployment method?
evidence: Startup script (synchronous): copies 400MB installer, then installs, before logon. Applied to OU=Workstations (800 machines).
Every boot waits for download+install. Monday 9 AM: 800 machines hammer the file server simultaneously.
choices: Synchronous startup scripts block logon until complete — a 400MB copy+install in the boot path is a guaranteed outage at scale. The right tool is software deployment designed for it: GPO Software Installation (assign, with its own scheduling), or better, a real deployment system (WSUS-like, PDQ, Intune, SCCM) with bandwidth management, scheduling, and reporting. Scripts are for configuration, not 400MB payloads
Make the script asynchronous so boot continues
Buy a bigger file server
Deploy at night via scheduled task instead
scenarios.why: Synchronous = the user waits; with 400MB × 800 machines the wait is 20 minutes and the file server melts under the Monday-morning thundering herd. Asynchronous scripts just hide the problem (installs race the user session, failures go unseen). A bigger file server treats the symptom; the design is still wrong. Nighttime scheduled tasks are closer but lack reporting, targeting, and retry — you have built a fragile deployment system by hand. The lesson is tool selection: GPO scripts are for lightweight configuration; software distribution needs a distribution system (scheduling, bandwidth control, status reporting, rollback). Using the wrong tool at scale converts an inconvenience into an outage.
scenarios.hint: Why are startup scripts the wrong tool for large software deployment?

scenarios.title: The filter that slowed logons
scenarios.situation: A WMI filter ('select only laptops with >8GB RAM') is linked to 6 GPOs. Logon times rose 45 seconds domain-wide. The filter query takes 8 seconds per evaluation on older machines.
evidence: SELECT * FROM Win32_ComputerSystem WHERE TotalPhysicalMemory > 8589934592 — evaluated per GPO per refresh.
6 GPOs × ~8s = ~48s added to foreground processing on slow machines.
choices: WMI filters evaluate synchronously during policy processing, and the cost multiplies per linked GPO — an 8-second query on 6 GPOs is 48 seconds of logon delay. Fix: replace with security-group targeting (evaluate group membership instead of hardware at logon — groups are cheap), or a single filtered GPO instead of six, or a faster query. WMI filters are for the exceptional case, not routine targeting
Buy faster machines
Increase the GPO refresh interval to reduce evaluations
WMI is broken; use registry preferences instead
scenarios.why: WMI filters run in the foreground policy path: every linked GPO pays the query cost, serially, on every refresh. An 8-second query feels harmless once; multiplied by 6 GPOs across every logon it is a 45-second tax on the whole domain. Faster hardware does not fix an O(n) design. Longer refresh intervals delay the pain but keep it (and slow policy convergence). Registry preferences do not target hardware at all. The professional fix is changing the targeting mechanism: security groups evaluate in milliseconds (the DC already knows membership). Reserve WMI filters for what groups cannot express (hardware attributes), keep them on as few GPOs as possible, and time your queries — if it takes seconds, it does not belong in the logon path.
scenarios.hint: Why do WMI filter costs multiply, and what is the cheaper alternative?

scenarios.title: The password in SYSVOL
scenarios.situation: Audit finds a Group Policy Preference with an embedded local-admin password (cpassword) in SYSVOL. It was set years ago 'temporarily.' SYSVOL replicates to every DC and is readable by all authenticated users.
scenarios.prompt: What is the severity and remediation?
evidence: Groups.xml in SYSVOL contains cpassword value. The AES key for cpassword was published by Microsoft years ago — decryption is a one-liner, known to every attacker.
Any domain user (any compromised workstation) can read and decrypt it. The password is the local admin on every machine the preference targeted.
choices: Critical: the cpassword AES key is public knowledge, so this is a plaintext-equivalent password readable by every authenticated user — assume every machine it touched is compromised. Remediate: remove the preference immediately, ROTATE the password everywhere it was deployed (it is burned), deploy LAPS for local admin passwords going forward, and hunt for lateral movement from those accounts
Low severity; the password is encrypted
Delete the preference; the problem is solved
Change the password on one machine as a precaution
scenarios.why: 'Encrypted' with a published key is not encrypted — Microsoft published the cpassword AES key, so decryption is trivial and universally known to attackers. This is functionally a plaintext domain-wide local-admin password. Deleting the preference stops future exposure but the password is already burned (assume it was harvested long ago — SYSVOL has been readable for years). Changing one machine misses the other N. The full response: kill the preference, rotate the credential EVERYWHERE it was pushed, move to LAPS (unique per-machine passwords, the designed solution), and investigate — a known local-admin password is a lateral-movement highway, so hunt for its use. Then grep every GPP XML in SYSVOL for cpassword remnants; where there is one, there are usually more.
scenarios.hint: Why is a cpassword 'encrypted' password actually plaintext?

domains.name: DNS & DHCP
domains.summary: Windows DNS zones and records, DHCP scopes and failover, and name-resolution troubleshooting.

scenarios.title: The website that moved
scenarios.situation: The company website migrated to a new host with a new IP Friday. Monday: half the office reaches the new site, half gets the old (dead) IP. The DNS record TTL was 24 hours; the change was made Friday 6 PM.
evidence: A record changed Fri 18:00, TTL 86400. Authoritative answers are correct everywhere.
Failing clients: ipconfig /displaydns shows the old IP cached. Working clients: fresh lookups or cleared caches.
choices: DNS caching layers: the 24h TTL means resolvers and clients cache the old record for up to a day after the change. Friday 6 PM + 24h = Saturday 6 PM expiry — but clients that looked up Friday afternoon hold it until their cache expires. Fix now: Clear-DnsClientCache on affected machines (or wait); fix forever: LOWER the TTL to 300s DAYS before a planned migration, then raise it after
The DNS change did not replicate; force replication
The old host is hijacking traffic; call the old provider
Half the clients have the wrong DNS server configured
scenarios.why: Every DNS answer carries a TTL — a license to cache. With a 24-hour TTL, any client that resolved the name Friday afternoon is entitled to keep the old answer until Saturday evening; 'half the office' is just the half that looked it up recently. The authoritative data is correct (replication is fine), nothing is hijacked, and the clients' server config is irrelevant. The operational lesson is the TTL dance: before any planned DNS change, lower the TTL to 5 minutes and wait out the old TTL, THEN make the change — migration completes in minutes instead of a day. Afterward, raise the TTL back. This is standard practice for every migration, and skipping it causes exactly this ticket.
scenarios.hint: What should you do to DNS TTLs BEFORE a planned migration?

scenarios.title: The vanishing records
scenarios.situation: Monday: random workstations lose network drives and fail logon. By Wednesday they work again. Pattern repeats weekly. DNS scavenging was enabled last month with 1-day no-refresh + 1-day refresh intervals.
evidence: No-refresh 1 day, refresh 1 day — aggressive. DHCP lease duration: 8 days.
Records disappear ~2 days after registration, reappear when the client re-registers (reboot/reconnect).
choices: Scavenging is deleting LIVE records: with DHCP leases of 8 days but scavenging intervals of 1+1 days, records become eligible for scavenging long before the client refreshes them. The no-refresh + refresh intervals must EXCEED the DHCP lease duration (standard: 7+7 days with 8-day leases). Set scavenging intervals longer than the lease, enable scavenging on the server AND the zone, and the 'random' outages stop
Scavenging is broken; disable it entirely
The workstations have a virus deleting DNS records
DHCP is misconfigured; shorten the lease to 1 day
scenarios.why: Scavenging deletes records whose timestamps are older than no-refresh + refresh — it cannot distinguish 'stale' from 'live but quiet' except by timestamp. With 1+1 day intervals and 8-day DHCP leases, a workstation that got its lease Monday and sits quietly has its record scavenged by Wednesday, long before the lease renews. Then drives disconnect (name no longer resolves) until something re-registers. Disabling scavenging trades the problem for zone bloat (the reason it was enabled). Shortening DHCP leases to match aggressive scavenging inverts the dependency and multiplies DHCP traffic. The rule: scavenging intervals > DHCP lease duration, always. And enable it deliberately on both server and zone — half-enabled scavenging is its own mystery.
scenarios.hint: What is the required relationship between scavenging intervals and DHCP lease duration?

scenarios.title: The mystery gateway
scenarios.situation: An entire floor loses internet but keeps LAN access. ipconfig shows gateway 192.168.1.1 (correct) on some machines, 192.168.1.99 on others. .99 is a home router someone plugged in 'to get better WiFi.'
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
evidence: Affected machines: DHCP server 192.168.1.99, gateway 192.168.1.99, DNS 192.168.1.99. Unaffected: DHCP from the real server.
Consumer router with DHCP enabled, plugged LAN-side into the corporate network.
choices: Rogue DHCP server: the home router answers DHCP Discovers (often faster than the real server — it is closer), handing out its own gateway/DNS. Clients route internet through a NAT box with no upstream. Fix now: unplug it; fix forever: DHCP snooping on switches (only trusted ports may serve DHCP), plus monitoring/alerting for unexpected DHCP servers
The corporate DHCP scope is full; expand it
The router is fine; configure it as the gateway
Reboot the affected machines; they will get correct leases
scenarios.why: DHCP is trust-based: clients accept the first Offer, and a rogue server on the local segment usually wins the race. The victims' config proves it — DHCP server .99, gateway .99, DNS .99 is the router's full fingerprint. A full scope would give APIPA addresses, not wrong gateways. Adopting the rogue router as infrastructure is surrender. Rebooting re-runs DORA — the rogue may win again. The durable fixes are at the switch layer: DHCP snooping drops DHCP offers from untrusted ports, which kills this entire attack class (accidental or malicious — a malicious rogue DHCP is also a credential-interception platform). Add port-security hygiene so unknown devices cannot join the LAN casually. 'Better WiFi' is how breaches start.
scenarios.hint: Why does the rogue server usually win the DHCP race?

scenarios.title: The conference-day outage
scenarios.situation: All-hands day: 400 visitors connect to the guest WiFi. By 10 AM new connections fail — 'no internet.' The guest scope is /24 (254 addresses) with 8-day leases. Regular days use ~100 addresses.
evidence: 192.168.99.0/24, 8-day lease, ~100 normal usage. Today: 400+ devices, scope exhausted by 10 AM.
Dozens of leases held by devices that left hours ago (8-day leases do not recycle intraday).
choices: Scope exhaustion from lease-duration mismatch: a /24 cannot serve 400 concurrent devices, and 8-day leases pin addresses to devices long gone. Fix: short leases for guest networks (1–4 hours — high churn needs fast recycling), a larger scope (expand to /23 or add scopes), and utilization alerts at 80%. The regular-day math hid the event-day reality
The WiFi access points are overloaded; add more APs
Visitors should use cellular data
Reboot the DHCP server to clear leases
scenarios.why: DHCP scope sizing has two variables: concurrent devices AND lease duration. A /24 with 8-day leases effectively serves ~254 devices per 8 days, not per moment — morning visitors' leases block afternoon visitors. The APs are fine (associated clients just cannot get IPs). 'Use cellular' is not an IT answer. Rebooting the server does not free leases (the database persists; and even 'reconcile' would be wrong while devices are gone). The design rule: guest/high-churn scopes get short leases (hours) so addresses recycle intraday, sized for peak concurrency plus headroom, with alerts before exhaustion. Size for the event, not the average — averages never attend all-hands day.
scenarios.hint: How do lease duration and scope size interact under churn?

scenarios.title: The slow internet
scenarios.situation: Internet browsing is intermittently slow; internal resources are fine. DNS forwarders point to the ISP's resolvers. Direct queries to 8.8.8.8 are fast; queries through the DCs sometimes take 2+ seconds.
evidence: nslookup via DC: intermittent 2s+ latency. Direct to 8.8.8.8: <50ms always. Internal zones: fast.
Forwarders: ISP DNS only. No conditional forwarders. Root hints untouched.
choices: Slow/unreliable forwarders: the DCs forward all external queries to the ISP resolvers, which are intermittently slow — every external lookup inherits the delay. Fix: replace or supplement forwarders with fast public resolvers (or use root hints), order by performance, and monitor forwarder response times. The DC is not slow; its upstream is
The DCs are underpowered; add CPU
Enable DNS caching with longer TTLs to mask it
The firewall is inspecting DNS; disable inspection
scenarios.why: The test isolates the layer: internal zones fast (server healthy), direct-to-8.8.8.8 fast (network path fine), via-DC slow (the forwarder path). The DC's CPU is irrelevant — it is waiting on the ISP, not computing. Longer client TTLs do not change the forwarder's latency for cache misses. Firewall DNS inspection is a guess without evidence. Forwarders are a dependency like any other: measure them (DNS performance counters, simple query timing), pick reliable ones, and have more than one decent option. Many shops forward to two providers or use root hints directly to remove the middleman. The general skill: when a chain is slow, test each link separately — the slow link is the one whose direct test is fast but whose chained test is slow.
scenarios.hint: How do you isolate a slow link in the DNS resolution chain?

scenarios.title: The printer that moves
scenarios.situation: The finance printer 'moves' IP addresses monthly, breaking everyone's mapped printer. It has a DHCP reservation — but the reservation is for the OLD network card; the printer's NIC was replaced twice.
evidence: Reservation: MAC AA:BB:CC (old NIC) → 192.168.1.50. Printer's current MAC: DD:EE:FF — gets a random dynamic lease.
NIC replaced twice; reservation never updated. Users remap the printer each time.
choices: Update the reservation to the printer's CURRENT MAC address — reservations bind MAC to IP, so a NIC swap silently voids them. Better: for infrastructure devices (printers, APs), use static IPs OUTSIDE the DHCP scope with documentation, or reservations with a process that updates them on hardware change. The root fix is the process: hardware changes must trigger reservation review
Delete the reservation; let the printer use dynamic DHCP
Give the printer a static IP inside the DHCP scope
Map printers by hostname instead of IP
scenarios.why: A reservation is a MAC→IP binding: replace the NIC and the binding points at a MAC that no longer exists, so the printer falls back to a dynamic lease while the reservation squats on .50 unused. Dynamic-only means the IP drifts (the original complaint). Static-inside-scope risks the DHCP server leasing .50 to a laptop (duplicate IP). Hostname mapping is good practice but does not fix the underlying address instability for direct-IP workflows. The durable answer: infrastructure devices get stable addresses by design — static outside the scope (with an exclusion/documentation) or maintained reservations — plus a hardware-change checklist that includes 'update DHCP reservations.' The ticket is never just about the printer; it is about the missing process.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when a reserved device's NIC is replaced?

scenarios.title: The name that resolves differently
scenarios.situation: app.corp resolves to 10.1.1.5 internally but the public DNS says 203.0.113.9 (the website). Internal users testing the new web deployment hit the internal app server instead of the new site — or is it the other way around? Nobody documented which is authoritative for whom.
evidence: Internal zone corp (AD-integrated) has app.corp = 10.1.1.5. Public DNS has app.corp = 203.0.113.9. Same name, two answers, no documentation.
Testers cannot tell which endpoint they hit; incidents get misdiagnosed by location.
choices: Undocumented split-brain DNS: the same name intentionally resolves differently inside/outside, but without documentation and a naming convention it becomes a troubleshooting trap. Fix: document the split-brain design explicitly (which names differ and why), prefer distinct names where possible (app-internal.corp vs app.corp), and ensure the right clients use the right view. Split-brain is legitimate; undocumented split-brain is a landmine
Delete the internal record; use the public IP everywhere
Delete the public record; the app is internal
DNS is broken; rebuild the zone
scenarios.why: Split-brain DNS (different answers inside vs outside) is a standard enterprise pattern — the failure here is not the technique but the missing documentation and the ambiguous naming. Deleting either record breaks a real use case (internal app access or public website). Rebuilding the zone destroys a working design to fix a documentation gap. The professional fix: make the invisible visible — document every split-brain name, its inside/outside answers, and the reason; use naming conventions that hint at scope (internal- prefixes); and verify client DNS paths so the right view reaches the right clients. When a name resolves differently by location, that fact belongs in the runbook, not in someone's head.
scenarios.hint: When is split-brain DNS correct, and what makes it dangerous?

domains.name: PowerShell Automation
domains.summary: The pipeline and objects, remoting, scripting, DSC, and execution policy.

scenarios.title: The script that parses Format-Table
scenarios.situation: A reporting script does Get-Service | Format-Table | Out-String, then uses regex to extract service names and statuses. It broke after a Windows update changed column widths. The author wants to 'fix the regex.'
evidence: $s = Get-Service | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String; then $s -match 'Running\s+(\S+)' — brittle text scraping.
Update widened the Status column; capture groups shifted; script reports wrong services.
choices: Stop formatting for machines: Format-* cmdlets are for human eyes — remove them from the pipeline and work with objects: Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' | Select-Object Name, Status. Properties do not shift with column widths; the script becomes immune to display changes
Fix the regex to handle the new column widths
Pin the Windows version so columns never change
Add -AutoSize with fixed widths to stabilize the output
scenarios.why: Format-Table renders for humans: column widths, truncation, and wrapping are display decisions that change between versions, consoles, and window sizes. Parsing that output with regex builds on sand — the update did not 'break' the script, it exposed that the script was always fragile. Pinning the OS version freezes the environment to protect a bad pattern. Fixed widths just move the fragility. The PowerShell-idiomatic fix: objects carry Name and Status as PROPERTIES, accessible regardless of display. Where-Object and Select-Object operate on data, not text. The rule: Format-* is always the LAST cmdlet, for eyes only, never piped into logic. Teach this once and a whole class of bugs disappears.
scenarios.hint: Why must Format-* never feed another cmdlet?

scenarios.title: The 500-server loop
scenarios.situation: An admin runs 1..500 | ForEach-Object { Enter-PSSession -ComputerName "srv$_"; Get-EventLog ...; Exit-PSSession } sequentially. It takes 6 hours. They ask for a faster server.
evidence: Sequential Enter/Exit-PSSession per server, one at a time, with session setup/teardown each iteration.
500 servers × ~40s (session setup + query + teardown) ≈ 5.5 hours. The server is idle; the admin's workstation waits on network round trips.
choices: The pattern is wrong, not the hardware: use Invoke-Command -ComputerName <all 500> { ... } — fan-out runs in parallel (default 32 at a time, tunable with -ThrottleLimit), sessions are managed efficiently, and results return as objects tagged with PSComputerName. Runtime drops from hours to minutes with zero new hardware
The admin workstation needs more CPU for the loop
Run it overnight as a scheduled task
Split the list across 5 admin workstations
scenarios.why: Sequential remoting pays full session-setup cost per server and waits idly between — the 6 hours are network waits, not computation, so a faster CPU changes nothing. Overnight scheduling hides the waste without removing it. Five workstations parallelize the bad pattern instead of fixing it. Invoke-Command's fan-out is the designed solution: one call, parallel execution, built-in throttling, aggregated object results. The broader lesson: when a script's runtime scales linearly with target count and the work is network-bound, the fix is parallelism at the tool level (fan-out, jobs, runspaces) — not hardware, not scheduling, not sharding the toil.
scenarios.hint: Why does sequential Enter-PSSession scale so badly, and what replaces it?

scenarios.title: The Remove-ADUser without WhatIf
scenarios.situation: A cleanup script disabled 200 stale accounts — plus 12 active ones, because the filter used LastLogonDate which is not replicated and stale on the queried DC. No -WhatIf run, no backup of the change set, no log.
evidence: Get-ADUser -Filter * | Where LastLogonDate -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-90) | Disable-ADAccount. Ran from a DC with stale replication.
12 active users disabled Monday morning; helpdesk chaos; no list of who was touched.
choices: Change control for destructive automation: (1) test the filter READ-ONLY first and eyeball the set, (2) run with -WhatIf, (3) capture the target list to a file BEFORE acting, (4) query LastLogonTimestamp (replicated) not LastLogonDate-via-one-DC, or check all DCs. Destructive scripts get a checklist, not a prayer — and the 12 users get re-enabled from the captured list, which should have existed
The script logic was correct; the DC was at fault
Disable-ADAccount is dangerous; avoid scripting it
Restore the 12 users from backup
scenarios.why: Two technical traps and one process failure: LastLogonDate from a single DC is non-replicated data (use LastLogonTimestamp, replicated, or query all DCs), and no -WhatIf/list-capture meant the blast radius was discovered via helpdesk tickets. But the root cause is process: destructive automation without a dry run, without a target list, without verification. 'The DC was at fault' blames documented behavior. Avoiding scripting surrenders the entire value of automation. Backup restore for 12 disables is overkill when re-enable suffices — IF you know who they are, which requires the list that was never captured. The rule: any script that disables/deletes/moves gets WhatIf + target-list + filter-verified-on-replicated-data, every time, no exceptions.
scenarios.hint: Which logon attribute is safe for stale-account detection, and why?

scenarios.title: The password in the script
scenarios.situation: A scheduled-task script contains $pass = ConvertTo-SecureString 'P@ssw0rd!' -AsPlainText -Force. It is in a git repo. Three admins have left since it was written.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exposure and fix?
evidence: Plaintext password in version control, replicated to every clone, in backup history forever.
Service account with local admin on 40 servers; password unchanged in 3 years.
choices: Full credential compromise: the password is in git history (undeletable), on every clone, readable by everyone with repo access — assume it is known. Fix: rotate the password immediately, remove it from the script, and use a gMSA (no password to store — the system manages it) or a credential vault (retrieve at runtime, never in code). Then audit the repo for other secrets
It is a SecureString, so it is encrypted and safe
Delete the line from the repo; history does not matter
Restrict repo access to current admins
scenarios.why: ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText -Force with a literal is plaintext with extra steps — the string sits in the file, in history, in every clone. SecureString protects memory, not source code. Deleting the line leaves it in git history (and every existing clone). Restricting access now does not un-expose the three departed admins' copies. The password is burned: rotate first, then fix the pattern. gMSA is the Windows-native answer (no stored password at all — ideal for scheduled tasks and services); a vault (CyberArk/HashiCorp Vault/Azure Key Vault) is the general answer. Then grep the repo for password/passwd/secret — where there is one, there are more. Secrets do not belong in code, ever.
scenarios.hint: Why does -AsPlainText -Force in source code provide zero protection?

scenarios.title: The config that keeps reverting
scenarios.situation: An admin manually installs a feature on a server; within 15 minutes it is uninstalled. They reinstall; it vanishes again. They suspect malware.
evidence: DSC pull configuration enforces 'Ensure = Absent' for that feature; LCM runs every 15 minutes.
Unaware DSC is configured; the 'malware' is the desired-state engine doing its job.
choices: DSC desired-state enforcement: the LCM detected drift from the declared configuration and remediated it — the feature is supposed to be absent per the config. This is DSC working correctly. Fix the CONFIGURATION (change Ensure to Present if the feature is wanted), not the server — hand-changes on DSC-managed nodes are futile by design
The server has malware; isolate and rebuild it
Disable the LCM so manual changes stick
The DSC pull server is misconfigured; shut it down
scenarios.why: Desired-state systems treat manual changes as drift to be corrected — the 15-minute cycle is the LCM consistency check, and 'reverting' is remediation, not infection. Calling it malware leads to a pointless rebuild that re-enrolls in DSC and reverts again. Disabling the LCM 'fixes' the symptom by destroying the enforcement the org deliberately built. Shutting down the pull server blinds the whole fleet. The correct mental model: on DSC-managed nodes, the configuration document is the truth — change the document, not the node. This generalizes to all config management (GPO, Intune, Ansible): fight the tool and you lose on schedule; update the declared state and the tool becomes your ally.
scenarios.hint: On a DSC-managed node, where do you make a configuration change?

scenarios.title: The module that works for me
scenarios.situation: A script runs on the admin's workstation but fails on the server: 'The specified module was not found.' The module lives in the admin's Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules.
scenarios.prompt: What is the module scope problem?
evidence: Module in user-scope path ($home\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules) — visible only to that user on that machine.
Script runs as SYSTEM via scheduled task; SYSTEM has no such path. $env:PSModulePath differs.
choices: Module scope: user-path modules are invisible to other users (especially SYSTEM) and other machines. Fix: install the module to the machine scope (Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules) or bundle it with the script/deployment. Design for the EXECUTION context, not the authoring context — test as the service account, on the target machine
Copy the module to the server's Documents folder
Run the task as the admin user instead of SYSTEM
Import the module with a hardcoded path in the script
scenarios.why: PowerShell module discovery is path- and user-dependent: Documents-based paths belong to one user on one machine. The script's execution context (SYSTEM, scheduled task, another server) has a different $env:PSModulePath and never sees it. Copying to another user's Documents repeats the fragility. Running as the admin 'fixes' it by widening the task's privilege (and breaks when the password changes). Hardcoded import paths work until the path moves. The robust patterns: machine-scope module installation (all users), or ship the module alongside the script with a relative import. And the meta-rule: always test in the execution context — 'works on my machine' is the #1 PowerShell deployment failure.
scenarios.hint: Why does a module visible to you vanish under a scheduled task?

scenarios.title: The silent failure
scenarios.situation: A provisioning script creates 50 users; 8 fail (duplicate sAMAccountName) but the script reports success and continues. The failures surface weeks later as access tickets.
evidence: New-ADUser calls without -ErrorAction Stop, no try/catch, no error log. Non-terminating errors print red text and continue.
'Success' with 8 missing users; discovered via downstream tickets.
choices: Errors must be caught and surfaced: wrap creation in try/catch with -ErrorAction Stop (converting non-terminating to terminating), log every failure with the identity and reason, and make the script EXIT NONZERO on any failure so automation/schedulers report it. A script that cannot fail loudly will fail silently — red text on a console nobody watches is not error handling
The script worked; the 8 duplicates are a data problem
Add -Verbose to see the errors better
Run the script again; the 8 will succeed now
scenarios.why: PowerShell's default error behavior (non-terminating: complain and continue) is designed for interactive use, not automation — in a script it means partial success reported as success. The duplicates ARE a data problem, but the script's job includes detecting data problems loudly. -Verbose adds noise without changing control flow. Re-running without fixing the duplicates reproduces the same 8 failures. The pattern for reliable automation: -ErrorAction Stop + try/catch around fallible operations, structured logging (what, which object, why), and a nonzero exit on failure so the scheduler/monitoring notices. Then fix the input data (pre-check for duplicates before creating). Silent partial failure is the most expensive bug class in provisioning.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between terminating and non-terminating errors in a script?

domains.name: Hyper-V Virtualization
domains.summary: Virtual switches, VHDX storage, checkpoints, replica, and VM performance.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM disk-full page
scenarios.situation: All VMs on HOST03 paused simultaneously at 3 AM. The host's CSV has 200GB free of 10TB — but the LUN underneath hit 100%: 40 VMs use dynamic VHDX, and a runaway log job grew several at once. The SAN admin says 'the host said it had space.'
evidence: Dynamic VHDX (thin) on CSV (thin) on thin-provisioned SAN LUN. Three thin layers, monitored at none.
LUN full → CSV paused I/O → all VMs paused. 200GB 'free' was CSV-level fiction over a full LUN.
choices: Stacked thin provisioning without end-to-end monitoring: each layer promised more than the layer below held. Dynamic VHDX is fine, but SOME layer must be monitored against physical reality — monitor the LUN (the bottom), alert the host at 80%, and either use fixed VHDX for predictability or enforce thin-provisioning budgets per layer. The fix is monitoring the physical truth, not any single layer's report
Convert all VHDX to fixed; thin provisioning is unusable
Add more SAN capacity and move on
The SAN is faulty; replace it
scenarios.why: Thin provisioning is a promise: each layer allocates on demand against capacity that may not exist. Stack three thin layers (dynamic VHDX → thin CSV/cluster volume → thin LUN) and the 'free space' each reports is relative to its own fiction — the only truth is the physical spindles. When the bottom fills, everything above pauses instantly and simultaneously. Fixed VHDX everywhere is one valid answer (predictability) but wastes the flexibility thin was bought for. More capacity without monitoring just moves the cliff. The professional posture: thin is allowed, but every thin layer gets a utilization alert against the layer below it, and capacity planning accounts for the overcommit ratio. Monitor the bottom.
scenarios.hint: Why did the host report free space while the VMs paused?

scenarios.title: The two-year-old checkpoint
scenarios.situation: VM SQL01 is mysteriously slow. Investigation: a checkpoint from 2 years ago ('BeforeUpgrade') still exists — the VM runs on a 2-year differencing chain. Merging will take hours and risks the production DB.
evidence: Checkpoint tree: 1 checkpoint, 26 months old, differencing chain 400GB deep. VM I/O does double duty (read base + write diff).
Created before an upgrade, never deleted. No checkpoint audit process.
choices: Checkpoint lifecycle failure: checkpoints are TEMPORARY change-rollback tools, not archives. A 2-year chain means every read potentially traverses the chain and every write extends it — the 'mystery' slowness is structural. Remediate: schedule a maintenance window, merge (delete the checkpoint), verify DB integrity after. Prevent: checkpoint aging alerts (>7 days = ticket), naming with expiry dates, and a rule that the change owner deletes their checkpoint
The storage is slow; migrate the VM to faster disks
Checkpoints are corrupt; restore from backup
Add more RAM to compensate for the I/O latency
scenarios.why: A checkpoint is a differencing disk: the VM's I/O now spans the base VHDX plus 26 months of diffs — reads scatter across the chain, and the chain only grows. Two years of 'temporary' is permanent by neglect. Faster disks would mask the structural cost. The checkpoint is not corrupt, just ancient — restore-from-backup is overkill for a merge operation. More RAM does not fix I/O path length. The operational lesson: every checkpoint needs an owner and an expiry. Name them 'PrePatch-2026-10-10-DELETE-AFTER-7D', alert on age, and make checkpoint cleanup part of the change ticket's closure criteria. The change is not done until its checkpoint is gone.
scenarios.hint: What is the performance cost of a long-lived checkpoint chain?

scenarios.title: The 32-vCPU VM that is slower than 8
scenarios.situation: A vendor demanded 32 vCPUs for their app VM. Performance got WORSE than the 8-vCPU config. The host has 2 NUMA nodes × 16 cores. The VM spans both nodes.
evidence: Host: 2 NUMA nodes, 16 cores each. VM: 32 vCPU — spans both nodes; memory split across nodes.
Remote memory access ~40% (cross-NUMA), CPU Ready time elevated (32 vCPUs harder to co-schedule).
choices: NUMA spanning + CPU scheduling cost: a 32-vCPU VM cannot fit in one NUMA node, so ~half its memory accesses cross the interconnect (slower), and the hypervisor struggles to co-schedule 32 vCPUs simultaneously (CPU Ready). The 8-vCPU VM fit in one node with local memory and easy scheduling. Fix: right-size to measured need (likely 8–12), enable NUMA topology exposure for legitimately large VMs, and never size by vendor demand without measurement
The host is underpowered; add a third NUMA node
Enable Hyper-Threading to get more cores
The vendor's app is single-threaded; nothing to do
scenarios.why: vCPUs are not free performance: beyond a NUMA node boundary, each additional vCPU buys cross-node memory latency, and large vCPU counts impose co-scheduling delays (the hypervisor waits for 32 physical cores to be simultaneously free). The 8-vCPU VM sat entirely within one NUMA node — all memory local, trivially schedulable. More NUMA nodes do not fix a VM that should not span. Hyper-Threading adds logical cores, not NUMA locality. 'Single-threaded' would argue for FEWER vCPUs, not 32. The discipline: start small, measure (CPU Ready, remote memory %), grow to evidence. Vendor sizing demands are starting points for testing, not architecture. Bigger is slower past the NUMA boundary — physics, not opinion.
scenarios.hint: What two costs does a VM pay for spanning NUMA nodes?

scenarios.title: The replica that replicated the ransomware
scenarios.situation: Ransomware encrypted the file server VM at 2 PM. The team fails over to the Hyper-V Replica copy — and finds it encrypted too. Replica interval was 5 minutes; the encryption took 40 minutes to complete.
evidence: 14:00 encryption starts; 14:40 completes. Replica faithfully copied every encrypted block within its 5-min interval. Failover at 15:00: encrypted replica.
Last real backup: 30 days ago ('we have Replica now').
choices: Replica is not backup: it replicates ALL changes including corruption, encryption, and deletions — with a 5-minute interval it is a near-real-time copy of the disaster. The team replaced backups with replication and lost both. Correct DR: Replica for host-failure failover PLUS independent versioned backups (immutable/offline) for data-corruption scenarios. Recovery now: rebuild from the 30-day backup (data loss) or pay/learn — and the lesson is architectural
The replica interval was too short; lengthen it to 24 hours
Failover was done wrong; the primary could be decrypted
Replica is broken; replace it with clustering
scenarios.why: Replication copies state; backup preserves history. A 5-minute replica of an encrypting VM is a 5-minute-delayed copy of the encryption — the interval length is irrelevant because the encryption took 40 minutes (any interval under 40 min copies it; a 24h interval just makes Replica useless for its actual job). The primary cannot be 'decrypted' by failover mechanics. Clustering would not help either (shared state, same corruption). The violated principle: every DR design must answer TWO questions — 'host died, how do we run?' (Replica/clustering) and 'data was corrupted, how do we go back?' (versioned, immutable backups). One mechanism cannot answer both. 'We have Replica now' retired the backups — that sentence was the disaster, weeks before the ransomware.
scenarios.hint: What two questions must every DR design answer?

scenarios.title: The migration that saturated the LAN
scenarios.situation: Live-migrating 10 VMs to the new host saturates the 1Gb management network; user traffic crawls for 2 hours. Migrations were started all at once over the management NIC.
scenarios.prompt: What is the migration-network design error?
evidence: Single 1Gb NIC: management + VM traffic + live migration, all converged.
10 concurrent migrations × GBs of RAM state = hours of saturation on the shared link.
choices: Live migration needs its own network: dedicate NICs/bandwidth to migration traffic (separate subnet, preferably 10Gb), stagger migrations (2–3 at a time, not 10), and never share the migration path with user/management traffic. The migrations were correct; the network design made them destructive
Live migration is too slow; use quick migration instead
Migrate at night only
The VMs have too much RAM; reduce it
scenarios.why: Live migration copies gigabytes of memory state over the wire — on a shared 1Gb management link, 10 concurrent migrations are a self-inflicted DDoS on your own users. Quick migration (pause-and-move) would have caused actual downtime instead of slowness — worse. Night-only scheduling avoids the symptom (users awake) without fixing the design (still saturates management). Reducing VM RAM to fit the network inverts the architecture. The design: migration traffic gets dedicated bandwidth (its own NICs/VLAN, 10Gb where possible), migrations are throttled (a few at a time), and constrained migration features (SMB/COMPRESSION options) tune the throughput. Infrastructure operations need their own lanes — management, migration, storage, and VM traffic separated, each sized for its job.
scenarios.hint: Why must live-migration traffic be network-isolated?

scenarios.title: The AV that scanned every VHDX
scenarios.situation: After deploying host-level antivirus with default settings, VM performance collapses. The AV scans every VHDX on every write — including the 2TB SQL data disk, continuously.
scenarios.prompt: What is the AV exclusion requirement for Hyper-V?
evidence: Default policy: scan all files on access. VHDX files: scanned on every host write (which is every guest write).
Host CPU saturated by scanning; guest I/O latency 10x. SQL timeouts.
