choices: Exclude virtualization files from host AV: VHDX/VHD/AVHDX, VM config directories, and the Hyper-V processes themselves (per Microsoft's AV exclusion guidance for Hyper-V). Scan INSIDE the guests with guest AV instead — the host sees only opaque disk blocks; scanning them is pure overhead with near-zero detection value. Then verify the exclusion list matches the vendor guidance exactly
Uninstall AV from the host; virtualization hosts do not need it
Move the VHDX files to a non-scanned drive letter
The SQL VM needs more resources to handle the scanning
scenarios.why: Host-level AV scanning VHDX files is scanning opaque blocks: the host cannot interpret the guest filesystem inside the VHDX, so it pays full scan cost for ~zero malware detection — while multiplying every guest write's latency. Uninstalling host AV entirely removes a real layer (the host OS itself needs protection). A 'non-scanned drive letter' is exclusion by obscurity, fragile and unaudited. More SQL resources feed the overhead instead of removing it. The correct architecture: host AV protects the host OS with virtualization-aware exclusions (VHDX, config paths, Hyper-V processes per vendor guidance), and guest AV protects inside each VM where the filesystem is visible. Two layers, each scanning what it can actually see. Verify exclusions after every AV policy change — defaults revert.
scenarios.hint: Why is host-scanning VHDX files pure overhead?

scenarios.title: The overcommitted host
scenarios.situation: HOST05 has 128GB RAM with 200GB assigned to VMs (Dynamic Memory). Under month-end load, VMs balloon, hosts page, and everything slows. The admin says 'Dynamic Memory handles overcommit.'
evidence: 128GB physical, 200GB assigned via Dynamic Memory. Month-end: actual demand ~150GB.
Ballooning, host paging, guest slowdowns. Dynamic Memory reclaims from idle VMs, but month-end has no idle VMs.
choices: Dynamic Memory is not magic capacity: it optimizes IDLE waste, but when real concurrent demand exceeds physical RAM, the host pages and every VM suffers. 200GB of promises against 128GB of RAM works only while 72GB+ stays idle simultaneously — month-end violates that. Fix: size for peak concurrent demand (not average), set realistic max caps per VM, monitor Memory Pressure counters, and keep N+1 headroom for failover
Dynamic Memory is broken; switch all VMs to static
Add a page file on SSD to handle the overflow
The month-end job needs optimization, not the host
scenarios.why: Dynamic Memory's promise — 'assign more than you have' — holds only when the overcommit is backed by actual idleness. It reclaims from idle VMs; when ALL VMs are busy (month-end), there is nothing to reclaim and the host hits the physical wall: paging, ballooning, collapse. Static memory everywhere would waste the idle-time efficiency without fixing peak sizing. SSD paging makes the collapse faster, not smaller. Optimizing the month-end job is fine but does not change the capacity math. The discipline: capacity-plan for PEAK CONCURRENT demand plus failover headroom; use Dynamic Memory for efficiency within that envelope; monitor the Memory Pressure counter (it predicts the wall before you hit it). Overcommit is a bet on idleness — know when the bet is off.
scenarios.hint: What assumption does memory overcommit depend on?

domains.name: File & Storage Services
domains.summary: NTFS and share permissions, DFS, quotas, and SMB security.

scenarios.title: The share nobody can write
scenarios.situation: Finance team cannot save to \\fs01\finance. Share permissions: Everyone Full Control. NTFS: Finance-Team Modify, inherited. The CFO's assistant (in Finance-Team) gets 'Access Denied' saving a spreadsheet.
evidence: Share: Everyone Full. NTFS on folder: Finance-Team Modify (OI)(CI). User: member of Finance-Team.
The FILE being overwritten was created by the CFO with explicit NTFS: CFO Full Control, inheritance BLOCKED on that file.
choices: The file's explicit ACL: inheritance is blocked on that specific spreadsheet, so the folder's Finance-Team Modify does not reach it — effective access on the FILE is CFO-only. The share and folder permissions are correct; the denial is at the file's broken inheritance. Fix: re-enable inheritance on the file (or add Finance-Team explicitly), then audit for other inheritance-blocked files
The share permissions are wrong; tighten them
The user is not really in Finance-Team; check group membership
NTFS is corrupted; run chkdsk
scenarios.why: Effective access evaluates at the OBJECT level: share (fine) → folder NTFS (fine) → file NTFS (broken inheritance, CFO-only). The most restrictive layer wins, and here the file's own ACL is the wall. This is why 'the share permissions are right but access is denied' almost always means: check inheritance on the specific object. Tightening share perms would make it worse. Group membership is a reasonable check but the evidence (only THIS file fails) points at the file. chkdsk is for filesystem corruption, not ACLs. The operational habit: when one file in a working share denies access, inspect that file's Security > Advanced > inheritance state first. And the meta-lesson: users breaking inheritance 'to protect' a file creates exactly these mysteries — train against it.
scenarios.hint: At which level is effective access actually evaluated?

scenarios.title: The deny that ate the department
scenarios.situation: To 'stop interns from deleting,' an admin added 'Interns — Deny Delete' on the department share root. Now NOBODY in the department (including managers) can delete files — managers are also in the Interns group from a onboarding mistake.
evidence: Deny Delete for Interns group on the root, inherited everywhere. Managers are nested in Interns.
Deny overrides all Allows: managers' Allow Delete is nullified by the inherited Deny.
choices: Deny ACEs override ALL allows, and group nesting makes them unpredictable: the managers inherited the Deny through accidental nesting. Fix: remove the Deny ACE entirely — design with Allows only (interns simply do not get Delete in their Allow set). Reserve Deny for rare explicit carve-outs, and audit group nesting before deploying any Deny
Remove the managers from the Interns group; the Deny is fine
Add an Allow Delete for Managers to override the Deny
Deny ACEs are broken; Microsoft should fix them
scenarios.why: Deny is absolute in Windows ACL evaluation: any matching Deny ACE kills the access regardless of how many Allows exist — there is no 'Allow overrides Deny.' Removing managers from Interns fixes today's symptom but leaves the landmine (the next nesting mistake re-triggers it). An 'Allow to override' cannot exist by design. The professional rule: build ACLs from Allows alone (if interns should not delete, their Allow set simply lacks Delete — no Deny needed). Deny is for exceptional carve-outs ('this one person must not, despite their groups'), deployed rarely, documented loudly, and reviewed regularly. Every Deny ACE is a future mystery; the best number of Deny ACEs is usually zero.
scenarios.hint: Why can no Allow ACE override a Deny?

scenarios.title: The namespace that pointed at a dead server
scenarios.situation: FS02 was decommissioned 6 months ago, but \\corp\shares\projects still lists it as a folder target. Clients occasionally get 'path not found' — the namespace still refers them to the dead server.
scenarios.prompt: What is the namespace hygiene failure?
evidence: Folder target \\FS02\projects still enabled. FS02: powered off, DNS record scavenged.
DFS referral includes the dead target ~50% of the time; those attempts fail before trying the live target.
choices: Stale folder target: decommissioning the server did not remove it from the DFS namespace — referrals still include the corpse. Fix: remove/disable the dead target in DFS Management (or PowerShell), verify referrals, and add 'remove DFS targets' to the server-decommission checklist. The namespace is only as healthy as its target list
DFS is unreliable; map drives directly to FS01
Clients are caching the referral; clear the cache everywhere
Rebuild the DFS namespace from scratch
scenarios.why: DFS referrals are built from the CURRENT target list: a dead target still listed gets referred to clients, who waste attempts on it (some fail outright before failover, some hang until timeout). The namespace did not 'go stale' — it was never updated, because server decommissioning and namespace hygiene are owned by different checklists (or no checklist). Direct mappings abandon the entire abstraction benefit. Client referral caches expire on their own; the server-side list is the problem. Rebuilding is overkill for a target-removal. The fix is process: the decommission runbook must include DFS target removal (plus DNS, monitoring, backups, AD computer object) — every name service that pointed at the server. Audit all namespaces for dead targets quarterly; this one hid for 6 months.
scenarios.hint: What must a server-decommission checklist include for DFS?

scenarios.title: The file that lost the conflict
scenarios.situation: Two users edit the same spreadsheet on different branch servers within minutes. DFSR replicates; one version wins, the other lands in ConflictAndDeleted. The loser redo their morning's work.
evidence: Multi-master, last-writer-wins, conflict loser to ConflictAndDeleted. No file locking across servers.
Shared spreadsheet, simultaneous edits at two sites — a collaboration pattern DFSR cannot safely support.
choices: DFSR has no distributed locking: concurrent edits to the same file on different members produce a conflict, and the loser is silently moved to ConflictAndDeleted — data loss by design for this workflow. Fix the WORKFLOW, not DFSR: single-writer patterns (edit on one server via the namespace), or a real collaboration platform (SharePoint/OneDrive with co-authoring) for multi-user files. DFSR is for distribution, not collaboration
DFSR is broken; open a support case
Shorten the replication interval so conflicts are rarer
Restore the loser from ConflictAndDeleted and merge manually each time
scenarios.why: Last-writer-wins is DFSR's documented conflict resolution — it is not malfunctioning, it is unsuitable for simultaneous multi-writer collaboration. Shorter intervals narrow the conflict window but cannot close it (two saves in the same minute still collide). Manual merges from ConflictAndDeleted institutionalize data loss as a process. The correct response is architectural honesty: DFSR distributes files to be READ at many sites and WRITTEN at one; multi-user concurrent editing belongs on platforms built for it (co-authoring with real locking/merging). When users lose work to ConflictAndDeleted repeatedly, the answer is never 'tune DFSR' — it is 'stop collaborating through a replication engine.'
scenarios.hint: What workflow is DFSR unsafe for, and what replaces it?

scenarios.title: The file screen that caught ransomware
scenarios.situation: At 9:03 AM, FSRM file screens start blocking .encrypted writes on the user share and emailing alerts. By 9:05, the source workstation is identified. Only 12 files were damaged before containment.
evidence: File screen blocking known ransomware extensions (*.encrypted, *.locked, etc.) with active notification.
9:03 first block+alert; 9:05 workstation isolated; 12 files affected; restored from backup by 9:30.
choices: File screens as a ransomware tripwire: blocking known-bad extensions does not PREVENT ransomware (new variants use new extensions), but it DETECTS the encryption behavior within seconds and identifies the source machine — converting a silent disaster into a 12-file incident. The win is detection speed + source attribution, paired with backups for the damaged files. Layer it: screens for detection, AppLocker for prevention, offline backups for recovery
File screens prevent ransomware; the network is now safe
The 12 files prove file screens do not work
Ransomware is unstoppable; the screens were luck
scenarios.why: File screens are a detective control, not a preventive one: they fire when the ransomware's behavior (writing .encrypted files) hits the screen — a brand-new extension sails through. Claiming prevention breeds complacency; dismissing the 12-file outcome misses the point (without the screen, the encryption runs for hours across the whole share). 'Unstoppable' is surrender dressed as realism. The value proposition is precise: seconds-to-detection, automatic source identification, and a bounded blast radius — which turns ransomware from a company-wide event into a reimage-and-restore ticket. Keep the screens updated (new extensions appear constantly), but never let them be the ONLY control. Defense in depth: prevent (AppLocker, patching), detect (screens, EDR), recover (immutable backups).
scenarios.hint: Are FSRM file screens preventive or detective against ransomware?

scenarios.title: The 2012 box in the corner
scenarios.situation: Vulnerability scan flags SMB1 enabled on FILEOLD (Server 2012, 'cannot be upgraded — runs the ancient ERP'). The ERP vendor is out of business. The server holds 10 years of financial archives.
evidence: SMB1 = EternalBlue-class exposure; FILEOLD is unpatched and unpatchable.
ERP needed quarterly for archive lookups; vendor dead; migration project unfunded.
choices: Isolate and mitigate, do not ignore: segment FILEOLD to a restricted VLAN (only the 3 archive users can reach it, no internet, no inbound from user LAN), disable SMB1 on EVERYTHING else, enforce SMB signing/encryption domain-wide, and document the risk acceptance with an owner and a migration plan (even unfunded — the plan must exist). 'Cannot upgrade' is a constraint to engineer around, not a permission to leave exposed
Leave it; the ERP is critical and it works
Upgrade it anyway; the ERP will probably survive
Disconnect it permanently; archives are not worth the risk
scenarios.why: 'It works' is not a security posture for an unpatchable SMB1 server — it is a WannaCry waiting for a phishing email. Forced upgrades of dead-vendor ERP risk the business process with no rollback. Permanent disconnection destroys a business capability (quarterly archive access is real). The professional answer is compensating controls: network segmentation shrinks the attack surface to 3 users, SMB1 disabled everywhere else removes lateral movement, and documented risk acceptance makes the residual risk explicit and owned (with a migration plan, because 'unfunded' is a budget decision that gets revisited). Legacy systems are managed, not wished away — isolation + documentation + a path forward.
scenarios.hint: How do you handle an unpatchable legacy server the business still needs?

scenarios.title: The disk that filled silently
scenarios.situation: The department share hits 100% Friday night; Monday's backups fail and users cannot save. No quotas were set — 'we have 10TB, that is plenty.' The culprit: a 3TB video render from an intern project.
evidence: 10TB volume, no quotas, no alerts. One 3TB file + normal growth = full.
Backup failures (no space for VSS), user saves failing, Monday chaos.
choices: Quotas AND alerts are capacity management: deploy FSRM quotas (hard or soft with notification) per department/user so no single writer can fill the volume, plus volume-level alerts at 80/90%. 'Plenty of space' is not a capacity plan — growth is certain, and the failure mode (full volume) breaks backups and saves simultaneously. The intern's video is not the villain; the missing guardrails are
Delete the video and ban video projects
Buy more storage
The backup software should handle full disks gracefully
scenarios.why: A volume without quotas is a commons: any single user can exhaust it, and the failure cascades (VSS needs space, so backups fail too — the safety net breaks exactly when you need it). Deleting the video fixes Friday; next month it is a database export. More storage without quotas just buys a bigger commons. Backup software cannot conjure disk space. The fix is structural: quotas bound individual consumption (soft quotas with warnings teach; hard quotas enforce), volume alerts fire BEFORE 100% (80% investigate, 90% act), and capacity reviews track growth trends. Storage administration is applied arithmetic: measure growth, project the fill date, act before it. 'Plenty' is not a number.
scenarios.hint: Why does a full volume break backups too?

domains.name: Patching & WSUS
domains.summary: WSUS architecture, update rings, servicing channels, and update troubleshooting.

scenarios.title: The patch that blue-screened payroll
scenarios.situation: Tuesday's cumulative update blue-screens 10% of machines with a specific storage driver. It was auto-approved to all rings simultaneously. Payroll processing is down.
evidence: Auto-approved for all computers; single ring ('All Computers'); deployed Tuesday 2 AM everywhere.
10% BSOD rate on one driver version; payroll down; no tested rollback beyond 'uninstall the update.'
choices: Ring discipline: the update went to the entire fleet at once with no pilot — a 10% failure rate hit production directly. Correct process: pilot ring (IT + canaries) for 3–7 days, broad ring next, servers last with maintenance windows; auto-approve ONLY after pilot validation (or auto-approve to pilot, manual promote). Rollback now: uninstall via script/GPO on affected, block the update, and the payroll outage is the tuition for rings
Microsoft's patch was bad; nothing could be done
The storage driver is at fault; blame the vendor
Disable Windows Update entirely to prevent recurrence
scenarios.why: Bad patches are a known constant — the variable is whether they hit your pilot or your payroll. Auto-approving to 'All Computers' converts Microsoft's QA miss into your outage with zero buffer. The driver vendor shares blame but you control your deployment. Disabling updates trades one outage for guaranteed future vulnerabilities. Rings exist precisely for this: the pilot ring's 10% BSOD rate would have been 5 machines, not payroll. The remediation sequence: stop the bleeding (decline/block the update), roll back affected (wusa /uninstall or scripted removal), then fix the process (rings, pilot validation, staged auto-approval). Every patch Tuesday is a controlled experiment — run it like one.
scenarios.hint: What is the purpose of a pilot ring?

scenarios.title: The console that takes ten minutes
scenarios.situation: The WSUS console takes 10 minutes to open; admins avoid it, so approvals lag months behind. The server runs WID, never maintained, with 5 years of superseded updates synced.
evidence: WID database bloated; 40k superseded updates; sync includes dead products; cleanup wizard never run.
Admins avoid the console → approvals lag → fleet unpatched → the slow console caused the security gap.
choices: WSUS care-and-feeding: run the Server Cleanup Wizard (decline superseded/expired, compress updates), reindex the WID/SUSDB (known script), trim products/classifications to what you need, and schedule it monthly. A tool too painful to use is a tool not used — the console's slowness directly produced the patching lag. Fix the maintenance, the compliance follows
WSUS cannot scale; migrate to another product
Buy a bigger server for WSUS
The admins are lazy; mandate console use
scenarios.why: This is a maintenance cascade: unmaintained database → unusable console → avoided administration → unpatched fleet. The root fix is boring operational hygiene, not a new product (which would need the same hygiene). Bigger hardware does not fix a bloated unindexed database. Mandating use of a 10-minute console mandates suffering, not compliance. WSUS specifically needs: declined superseded updates (they accumulate forever otherwise), periodic reindexing (the documented WID maintenance), product/classification pruning (every dead product is sync time and DB rows), and the cleanup wizard on a schedule. Put it in the monthly maintenance calendar with an owner. Tools are kept usable or they are abandoned — there is no third option.
scenarios.hint: Why does an unmaintained WSUS directly cause unpatched machines?

scenarios.title: The update stuck at 0%
scenarios.situation: A VIP's laptop has been 'downloading updates' at 0% for 3 days. The helpdesk wants to reimage it. The user has a board presentation tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: What is the measured troubleshooting path?
evidence: Windows Update stuck 0%, 3 days. Other updates install fine on peers.
Can reach WSUS (:8530 open); GPO applied; SoftwareDistribution folder 12GB with ancient partial downloads.
choices: Reset the Windows Update components properly: stop wuauserv/bits/cryptsvc, rename SoftwareDistribution/Catroot2 (do not delete — rename for forensics/rollback), restart services, rescan. The 12GB of corrupt partial state is the likely culprit; a reset clears it in minutes. Reimaging is hours of user pain for a 10-minute fix — escalate to reimage only if component reset + DISM/SFC fail
Reimage immediately; 3 days is enough troubleshooting
Wait another day; it might finish
The laptop is too old; replace it
scenarios.why: Stuck-at-0% with a bloated SoftwareDistribution is the textbook corrupted-update-state signature — the fix is a component reset, measured in minutes, with rename-not-delete preserving evidence. Reimaging for this is using a sledgehammer on a finishing nail: hours of user downtime, data migration risk, and app reinstalls, the night before a board presentation. Waiting is hope, not a plan. Hardware replacement for a software-state issue is budget-burning. The methodology matters more than this ticket: diagnose before escalating (connectivity → policy → client state → corruption, in order), and match the fix to the layer. The helpdesk's instinct to reimage is the process failure to train out — reimage is the LAST resort, not the first.
scenarios.hint: What is the correct escalation order for a stuck update?

scenarios.title: The branch that never patches
scenarios.situation: The branch office (200 machines, downstream replica WSUS) shows 0% compliance for 4 months. The replica syncs from upstream, but approvals never arrive. The replica was configured as 'autonomous' by mistake.
evidence: Upstream: approves updates. Downstream replica set to Autonomous — it does NOT inherit approvals, and nobody approves locally.
Updates sync (content present) but nothing is approved — clients see no applicable updates. 4 months silent.
choices: Replica mode mismatch: an Autonomous downstream requires LOCAL approvals, which nobody performs — it sits at 0% forever. Fix: set it to Replica mode (inherits upstream approvals — central control) OR keep Autonomous and assign a local approver with a process. The deeper failure is 4 months of 0% compliance with no alert — compliance reporting must be monitored, not just generated
The replica is broken; rebuild it
Branch clients should point to the upstream WSUS directly
WSUS cannot do branches; use another tool
scenarios.why: WSUS downstream modes are a governance choice: Replica = central approvals flow down (one decision, fleet-wide); Autonomous = local approvals (branch control, local responsibility). 'Autonomous' with no local approver is the worst of both — no central control AND no local action. Content syncing fine while approvals sit empty is the signature: the pipe works, the decisions do not. Pointing branch clients at upstream wastes WAN and does not fix the mode confusion. The meta-failure dwarfs the config error: 4 months at 0% compliance means nobody looked at the report. Compliance dashboards need alerting (compliance < threshold = ticket), not just existence. Fix the mode today, fix the monitoring this week.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between Replica and Autonomous downstream servers?

scenarios.title: The eternal pending reboot
scenarios.situation: 30% of workstations show 'pending reboot' for updates installed weeks ago. Users keep deferring. Two of those machines were compromised via a vulnerability patched (but not rebooted into effect) a month ago.
evidence: Updates installed, reboot pending indefinitely. No deadlines configured; users defer forever.
Compromise via CVE fixed by the pending update — installed but not effective without the reboot.
choices: Deadlines: an installed-but-pending update is NOT protection — the vulnerable code runs until reboot. Configure update deadlines via GPO (e.g., 3 days after install, with user notifications and a final forced reboot), so deferral is bounded. The two compromises are the tuition: 'pending reboot' is an unpatched machine wearing a patched disguise
Users need security training about rebooting
Reboot all machines nightly by force
The updates are faulty if they need reboots
scenarios.why: A pending reboot is a Schrödinger's patch: installed on disk, absent from memory — the running kernel/drivers are still the vulnerable ones. Training asks users to voluntarily accept disruption; deadlines make disruption bounded and predictable (notify at 3 days, warn at 1, reboot with a final countdown). Nightly forced reboots punish users and still allow a 24h window; deadlines are the calibrated tool. 'Needs reboot' is not a fault — it is how OS patching works. The policy: deadlines configured, notifications clear, exceptions documented (the 24/7 machine gets a maintenance window, not an exemption). Measure 'reboot compliance' alongside 'install compliance' — the report that matters counts effective patches, not downloaded ones.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'installed, pending reboot' not the same as patched?

scenarios.title: The driver update that broke printing
scenarios.situation: WSUS auto-approved a printer driver update; 200 printers stopped working Friday afternoon. The driver was classified under 'Drivers' which syncs automatically.
scenarios.prompt: What is the driver-update policy lesson?
evidence: Drivers classification synced + auto-approved. No pilot for drivers.
200 dead printers, Friday PM, helpdesk meltdown. Rollback = manual driver reinstall per machine.
choices: Drivers are not patches: exclude the Drivers classification from auto-approval (sync selectively or not at all), pilot driver updates like any change, and prefer vendor-managed driver deployment for printers. OS security updates and hardware drivers have completely different risk profiles — the approval process must reflect that. Roll back now (decline + scripted reinstall of the good driver), then fix the classification policy
Printers are unreliable; replace them
Microsoft should not ship driver updates
Disable printing until Monday
scenarios.why: Driver updates carry hardware-specific regression risk far beyond OS patches: a bad cumulative is rare and broad; a bad driver is common and device-specific. Auto-approving the Drivers classification hands that risk to every machine simultaneously — Friday afternoon, naturally. The correct policy: do not sync Drivers in WSUS at all for most fleets (manage drivers via vendor tools, OS inbox drivers, or targeted deployment), and if synced, never auto-approve. Printers are the classic victim because printer drivers are notoriously fragile. The broader principle: approval policy should match the change's risk profile — one auto-approval rule for everything is how 200 printers die at 4 PM on Friday.
scenarios.hint: Why should driver updates have a different approval path than OS updates?

scenarios.title: The 2012 R2 in production
scenarios.situation: Three production servers run Windows Server 2012 R2 — end of support. They run a legacy app with no migration path. The security team demands they be patched; there are no patches.
evidence: 2012 R2, EOS, unpatchable, production, legacy app, no vendor.
Extended Security Updates (paid, time-limited), isolation, migration.
choices: Layered reality check: (1) evaluate Extended Security Updates as a BRIDGE (paid, temporary — it buys time, not a future); (2) isolate aggressively (dedicated VLAN, firewall to only required flows, no internet, enhanced monitoring); (3) fund and execute the migration (the app must move — 'no path' means 'no path YET'); (4) document risk acceptance with an owner and expiry. 'Cannot patch' is managed like the SMB1 legacy box: compensating controls + a real path forward, not acceptance by silence
Leave them; they have run fine for years
ESU forever; the fee is cheaper than migration
Power them off; security beats availability
scenarios.why: 'Running fine for years' is survivorship bias with a CVE list growing monthly — unpatched servers are compromised eventually, not hypothetically. ESU as a permanent strategy is renting time at increasing cost while the skills and drivers decay around you. Powering off destroys the business capability the servers exist for. The honest handling names the situation: these are legacy systems in managed decline. ESU bridges (1–3 years), isolation shrinks exposure, monitoring watches the reduced surface, and the migration gets a funded plan with dates — because the only actual fix is leaving the platform. Document it all: risk acceptance with an owner, an expiry date, and a migration milestone. Silence is the real vulnerability.
scenarios.hint: What is the role of Extended Security Updates in a legacy plan?

domains.name: Monitoring & Diagnostics
domains.summary: Event logs, Performance Monitor, alerting, and centralized monitoring.

scenarios.title: The cleared log
scenarios.situation: Monday: the Security log on FILE01 was cleared Sunday 2 AM (event 1102 on the DC's forwarded events). No change ticket, no admin admits to it. The file server holds payroll data.
evidence: Event 1102 (audit log cleared) on FILE01, Sunday 02:13. Preceded by 3 failed logons (4625) for a service account from an unusual IP.
Payroll data; no authorized maintenance window Sunday.
choices: Treat as a security incident: 1102 + preceding 4625s + no change record = probable compromise with log-tampering. Isolate FILE01 (network, not power — preserve memory), preserve forwarded events (they survived — central collection just paid for itself), engage the incident process, and hunt: what did the service account touch? Do NOT just re-enable auditing and move on
Someone ran wevtutil by mistake; re-enable logging and move on
The log filled up and auto-cleared; increase the log size
Restore the log from backup
scenarios.why: Event 1102 is one of the highest-fidelity malicious indicators in Windows: legitimate admins rarely clear security logs, and never at 2 AM on a Sunday without a ticket. The preceding 4625s (failed logons for a service account from an unusual IP) complete the story — attempted access, then evidence destruction. 'Mistake' does not explain the 4625s. Logs do not auto-clear to 1102 (overwrite is silent; 1102 is explicit clearing). You cannot restore a cleared log from backup usefully for forensics of the gap. The forwarded events on the collector are the lifeline — this is WHY logs are forwarded centrally. Incident process now: isolate, preserve, hunt, remediate. And afterward: alert on 1102 everywhere, immediately, always.
scenarios.hint: What makes event 1102 a high-fidelity incident indicator?

scenarios.title: The slow server with no baseline
scenarios.situation: USERS complain FILE02 is 'slow.' CPU 40%, memory 60%, disk queue 12, disk latency 180ms. The admin wants to add RAM. There is no baseline — nobody measured FILE02 when it was healthy.
evidence: CPU 40% (fine), memory 60% (fine), disk queue 12 + 180ms latency (terrible — healthy is <10ms, queue <2).
No baseline; 'slow' started gradually over months.
choices: Disk subsystem bottleneck: 180ms latency and queue depth 12 say the disks cannot keep up — CPU and memory are innocent. Adding RAM fixes nothing (memory is not the constraint). Diagnose the storage: RAID health? Failing disk? Dedup/snapshot overhead? Backup window overlap? Then fix the storage layer. And start baselining — without 'normal,' every future ticket starts blind
Add RAM; memory pressure is the usual cause
Add CPU; 40% is nearly half
The network is slow; check the switch
scenarios.why: The counters name the culprit plainly: disk latency 180ms (healthy: single-digit ms) with a queue of 12 means I/O requests wait ~180ms each — everything file-serving queues behind storage. CPU at 40% and memory at 60% are bystanders. More RAM does not speed disks. More CPU does not speed disks. The switch is innocent (latency is disk, not network). The gradual onset over months suggests degradation (failing disk in RAID, growing fragmentation, dedup backlog) rather than a config change — check RAID status and disk SMART first. The meta-lesson: baselines turn 'slow' into '180ms vs our 6ms baseline, started March' — a diagnosis instead of a guess. Capture baselines at build; this ticket would have been a 10-minute comparison.
scenarios.hint: Which counter identifies the bottleneck here, and what are its healthy values?

scenarios.title: The service that dies quietly
scenarios.situation: The line-of-business service stops every few weeks; users notice before IT does. Event log shows 7034 (service terminated unexpectedly) each time. No alert exists — 'we check it in the morning.'
evidence: 7034s in System log, weeks apart, no pattern. Service recovery actions: not configured (Take No Action).
User reports, 30–60 min after each failure. No SCOM/agent alert, no recovery action.
choices: Two missing layers: (1) service recovery actions (restart on first/second failure — self-healing for transient crashes), and (2) alerting on 7034/7000/7001 for this service (detection in seconds, not user-reports). 'Check it in the morning' is not monitoring. Configure recovery + alert, then investigate the root cause of the crashes (the 7034s have a pattern — memory leak? dependency?) — alerting without root-causing is pagers without progress
The service is buggy; ask the vendor for a fix and wait
Have the helpdesk check it hourly
Restart the service on a nightly schedule to preempt the crashes
scenarios.why: User-reported outages are the most expensive detection method (30–60 min of downtime plus reputation). Recovery actions are built into every Windows service and take 2 minutes to configure — first failure: restart; second: restart; subsequent: alert. Event-driven alerting on 7034 turns detection from 'users call' to 'ticket in 60 seconds.' Hourly human checks do not scale and miss the window anyway. Nightly restarts mask the root cause (and cause a nightly blip). The vendor may indeed owe a fix — but 'wait for the vendor' while users detect your outages is not a posture. Monitor now (recovery + alert), root-cause in parallel (crash dumps, memory trend — the 7034s weeks apart smell like a slow leak). Detection first, diagnosis second, vendor third.
scenarios.hint: What are the two missing layers for a quietly-dying service?

scenarios.title: The alert that cried wolf
scenarios.situation: The disk-space alert fires 20 times a day for a volume that hovers at 91% (threshold 90%). The team muted the alert channel. Last night a DIFFERENT volume filled to 100% and nobody noticed — backups failed.
evidence: Threshold 90%, volume sits at 91% chronically — 20 alerts/day, all 'known.' Channel muted.
Volume B hit 100% overnight; its alerts went to the muted channel. Backup failures discovered at 8 AM.
choices: Threshold without hysteresis and without actionability: a 90% threshold on a volume living at 91% generates noise, noise gets muted, and muting blinds the real event. Fix: alert on TREND + threshold (e.g., 90% AND growing >5%/day, or 95% absolute), add hysteresis (clear at 85%), separate 'warning' from 'critical,' and NEVER mute a channel — tune the alert instead. The 100% volume is the tuition for alert hygiene
Raise the threshold to 95% so it fires less
The monitoring tool is too noisy; replace it
Assign someone to watch the dashboard all day
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a safety-system failure: the team did the rational thing (muted noise) and the system did the predictable thing (missed the real event). Raising the threshold to 95% just moves the noise line — the volume will hover at 96%. Replacing the tool keeps the bad thresholds. Human dashboard-watching does not scale and misses nights. The fix is alert DESIGN: thresholds with hysteresis (fire at 90, clear at 85 — no flapping), trend-aware conditions (filling fast matters more than sitting high), severity tiers (warning vs critical vs page), and a monthly review that deletes or tunes noisy alerts. An alert that fires 20 times a day for a known state is not an alert — it is spam with a severity label. Every alert must be actionable, or it must not exist.
scenarios.hint: What turns a threshold alert into noise, and what fixes it?

scenarios.title: The replication nobody watched
scenarios.situation: repadmin /replsummary during an incident shows one DC with 'largest delta 45 days' — it stopped replicating 45 days ago. Nobody noticed. Password changes on other DCs never reached it; its logons use 45-day-old data.
scenarios.prompt: What monitoring gap allowed 45 days of silent failure?
evidence: DC03: replication failing 45 days (target principal name incorrect — machine account password mismatch, classic). Still serving logons with stale data.
No repadmin checks, no replication alerts. dcdiag never run proactively.
choices: Replication health monitoring: repadmin /replsummary or /showrepl on a schedule with alerting on failures/deltas, plus dcdiag in the monitoring baseline. Replication failures are SILENT to users (logons still work — with stale data) until they become catastrophic (lingering objects, auth failures). 45 days means the tombstone lifetime is approaching — this is now a recovery project, not a monitoring fix. Fix the trust (reset machine account), then ensure it can never go 45 days unnoticed again
Demote and repromote DC03; replication will be fine
Replication is not critical; logons work
Manually force replication once; it will catch up
scenarios.why: Replication failure is the silent killer of AD: everything appears to work (logons succeed — against stale data) while the directory diverges. At 45 days you are near tombstone lifetime (default 180 days, but lingering-object risk grows); a simple 'force sync' can reanimate deleted objects as lingering ghosts. Demote/repromote without diagnosing wastes the learning (the cause was a machine-account password mismatch — fixable). 'Logons work' is exactly why it went 45 days — the failure mode is invisible without monitoring. The non-negotiable: replication health is a monitored metric (replsummary deltas, failure counts), checked daily by automation, alerted on deviation. AD without replication monitoring is a distributed system you hope is consistent.
scenarios.hint: Why can replication fail for weeks without user complaints?

scenarios.title: The certificate that expired silently
scenarios.situation: The RDS gateway certificate expired Saturday. Monday: 300 remote users cannot connect. No expiry monitoring existed — 'we thought the CA auto-renewed.' It did not; auto-enrollment was never configured.
scenarios.prompt: What is the certificate lifecycle gap?
evidence: RDS GW cert expired Saturday 00:00. No monitoring, no auto-enrollment, no calendar entry.
300 remote users down Monday morning; emergency cert issuance under pressure.
choices: Certificate lifecycle management: inventory all certs with expiry dates, monitor at 90/60/30/7 days, and prefer auto-enrollment/auto-renewal where the CA supports it. A certificate is a time bomb with a readable timer — the only failure is not reading it. Emergency issuance under outage pressure is how wrong SANs and weak keys happen; planned renewal is boring and correct
Certificates should last longer; buy 5-year certs
The CA is unreliable; switch CAs
Users should have reported it Saturday
scenarios.why: Every certificate carries its expiry in plaintext — there is no excuse for surprise. Five-year certs just make the surprise rarer and the key older (and modern practice is SHORTER lifetimes, not longer). The CA did not fail; it was never asked to auto-renew. Users cannot report what they cannot see coming (and Saturday had no users). The fix is a lifecycle, not a purchase: centralized inventory (script it — query the bindings), expiry alerting with escalating lead times, auto-enrollment for domain-joined workloads, and a calendar owned by a human for the exceptions. Certificates are one of the few failure modes that announce themselves months in advance — honor the announcement.
scenarios.hint: What are the three layers of certificate expiry defense?

scenarios.title: The green backup that was not
scenarios.situation: The backup dashboard is green: jobs 'succeed' nightly. During a file-restore request, the admin discovers the last 3 months of 'successful' backups contain no data — the agent was backing up an empty mount point after a drive-letter change.
evidence: Status: Success, 90 days. Data: empty (source path wrong after drive letter reassignment).
Only when a real restore was requested — 3 months too late.
choices: Restore testing and backup content verification: 'success' meant the job ran, not that data was captured. The missing layers: (1) verify backup SIZE/content trends (a backup that drops to near-zero bytes is screaming), (2) periodic TEST RESTORES (the only proof), (3) alert on anomaly (size delta > threshold). A backup system measures restores, not job completions — reframe every report around 'last successful restore test'
The backup software is faulty; replace it
The drive letter change was unauthorized; find who did it
Backups are unreliable; keep multiple copies
scenarios.why: Job-success is a process metric; restore-success is the outcome metric — and they diverged for 90 days because nobody checked the outcome. The drive-letter change is a normal operational event; the backup system's job is to survive normal events (or alert loudly when its source vanishes — backing up an empty path 'successfully' is the software's failure too). Multiple copies of empty backups are empty. The layered fix: content-aware checks (size trends, file counts — a backup that shrinks 99% overnight pages someone), scheduled test restores (weekly file-level, quarterly system-level), and reports reframed as 'last verified restore: <date>' instead of 'last job status: success.' Trust, but verify — especially the thing everything depends on.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between backup job success and backup success?

domains.name: Server Core, Roles & Networking
domains.summary: Server Core vs Desktop Experience, roles and features, NIC teaming, and Storage Spaces.

scenarios.title: The Core server nobody can administer
scenarios.situation: A new DC was built as Server Core. The admin RDPs in, sees a command prompt, panics, and requests a rebuild 'with the GUI.' The server is in production.
evidence: Server Core, healthy, AD DS running. Admin's toolkit: RDP + hope.
No RSAT on the workstation, no Windows Admin Center, no remoting habit — the admin's skills assume a local GUI.
choices: Remote administration, not rebuild: install RSAT on the admin workstation, point Server Manager/MMCs at the Core server, enable PowerShell remoting, optionally deploy Windows Admin Center. Rebuilding Core→GUI for admin comfort surrenders the smaller attack surface and patch footprint for a skills gap — close the gap instead. The server is fine; the toolkit is incomplete
Rebuild with Desktop Experience; Core is impractical
Install the GUI on the Core server
Hire a Core specialist
scenarios.why: Server Core is the same OS minus Explorer — every administrative function remains available remotely. The panic comes from an admin whose entire workflow is 'RDP and click,' which Core deliberately breaks. Rebuilding to GUI trades permanent security/patching cost for temporary comfort. Converting Core→GUI in place is possible but concedes the design. A specialist hire for one server is absurd. The actual fix is the standard management stack every Windows shop should have anyway: RSAT on workstations, remoting enabled fleet-wide, WAC for the visual thinkers. Build the stack once and Core becomes easier than GUI — scriptable, repeatable, and administrable without RDP at all.
scenarios.hint: What is the standard management stack for Server Core?

scenarios.title: The server that does everything
scenarios.situation: SRV01 runs AD DS, DNS, DHCP, file shares, print services, AND WSUS. It needs a reboot for patching; the change board balks — rebooting takes down identity, name resolution, addressing, files, printing, and patching at once.
evidence: 6 roles, one box. Reboot impact: the entire infrastructure stack. Patching requires a full-outage change ticket.
'It was just for testing' — 4 years ago.
choices: One server, one role (mostly): combined roles fuse failure domains and maintenance windows — you cannot patch DHCP without rebooting the DC, cannot troubleshoot files without touching identity. Fix: separate into role-appropriate VMs (DCs, file server, WSUS each isolated), which virtualization makes nearly free. The 'temporary' consolidation became permanent because nobody scheduled the separation — schedule it now, migrate role by role
It works; document the reboot procedure and keep it
Buy a bigger SRV01 so it reboots faster
Disable patching to avoid the reboots
scenarios.why: Role consolidation feels efficient until maintenance: every patch, every reboot, every troubleshooting session carries the blast radius of ALL roles. The change board's fear is rational — the design made routine maintenance dangerous. Documentation does not shrink blast radius. Bigger hardware reboots marginally faster. Skipping patches trades availability theater for vulnerability reality. Virtualization exists precisely to end this tradeoff: separate VMs per role cost little and restore independent lifecycles (patch WSUS Tuesday, reboot the file server Wednesday, never touch the DCs together). The migration is unglamorous role-by-role work — which is why 'temporary' lasted 4 years. Put it on the project list with dates.
scenarios.hint: Why does role consolidation make patching dangerous?

scenarios.title: The team that was not
scenarios.situation: A host has NIC teaming configured (LACP). During a switch firmware upgrade, the host loses all network. Investigation: the switch side was never configured for LACP — the 'team' was two independent NICs, and the upgrade took down the one carrying traffic.
evidence: Host: LACP team of 2 NICs. Switch: ports in access mode, no LACP.
'We have teaming' — believed for 2 years, never failover-tested.
choices: The teaming was fictional: LACP requires BOTH sides configured — host-only LACP against access ports is not a team, it is two NICs with a shared name. The host sent LACPDUs into the void; traffic used one NIC; the upgrade killed that path. Fix: match the modes (Switch Independent needs no switch config — simplest; or configure LACP on the switch properly), then TEST failover (disable one NIC, watch traffic continue). Untested resilience is not resilience
Teaming does not work; remove it
The switch firmware upgrade was at fault
Add a third NIC for safety
scenarios.why: Network resilience has two halves: configuration AND validation. The config was half-done (host LACP, switch access — a mismatch that 'works' by accident on one NIC), and validation was never done (2 years, zero failover tests). The firmware upgrade merely exposed the fiction. Removing teaming surrenders the goal. Blaming the upgrade misses that a correct team survives switch work. A third NIC triples the misconfiguration. The fix pattern: choose the SIMPLEST teaming mode your switches support without special config (Switch Independent/Dynamic), verify the team actually fails over (pull a cable in maintenance), and re-verify after every switch change. Resilience is a tested property, not a configured one.
scenarios.hint: Why must teaming modes match on both ends, and what proves a team works?

scenarios.title: The parity volume under SQL
scenarios.situation: A new SQL Server's data volume is Storage Spaces parity ('we wanted capacity'). Transaction latency is terrible; the DBA blames the SAN. The volume is local parity spaces.
evidence: 4-disk parity space hosting SQL data files. Write penalty: parity requires read-modify-write per write.
SQL Server: random small writes, latency-sensitive — the worst case for parity.
choices: Parity is for capacity, mirror is for performance: parity's read-modify-write penalty destroys transactional write latency. SQL data/log volumes want MIRROR (or hardware RAID10 equivalent) — the capacity cost is the price of the workload's physics. Move SQL to a mirrored space; relegate parity to backups, archives, and file shares (sequential, capacity-hungry). The DBA was right to complain, wrong about the layer
Add more disks to the parity space
SQL needs tuning; the storage is fine
Move SQL to the SAN
scenarios.why: Parity RAID writes require reading old data + old parity, computing new parity, writing both — 4 I/Os per write, plus CPU. For sequential bulk writes (backups) that is fine; for SQL's random small writes it is latency poison. More disks widen the stripe without removing the per-write penalty. SQL tuning cannot fix storage physics. The SAN is not involved (local spaces) — and moving to SAN just relocates the question (the SAN would need RAID10 too). The rule: match resiliency type to workload — mirror for latency-sensitive transactional (SQL, Exchange), parity for capacity-sequential (backups, archives). Storage design starts from the workload's I/O pattern, not from the capacity wish list. Measure the workload first (DiskSpd, PerfMon), then choose.
scenarios.hint: Why is parity wrong for SQL data files?

scenarios.title: The WAC gateway with no MFA
scenarios.situation: Windows Admin Center gateway is deployed for the team — with Windows auth only, no MFA, accessible from the user LAN. It manages every server including DCs.
evidence: Gateway with full admin rights to all servers, single-factor auth, user-LAN reachable.
Compromise one admin's workstation/password → browse to WAC → full fleet control via a web UI.
choices: The WAC gateway is a privilege-concentration point: it must be hardened like the access it grants — restrict to the admin VLAN/workstations, require MFA (or smart card), limit gateway admins, audit its use. A single-factor web UI to the whole fleet from the user LAN collapses every tier boundary: the attacker skips the workstation-to-DC path entirely and drives the fleet from a browser
WAC is insecure; uninstall it
Admins should use strong passwords; that is enough
Move WAC to the internet for easier access
scenarios.why: Privileged access tools inherit the privilege of everything they manage: WAC with fleet-wide admin is, functionally, a Domain Admin credential with a web interface. Single-factor auth on it means the entire tier model reduces to one password. User-LAN reachability means any compromised workstation is one browser tab from the DCs. Strong passwords help but single-factor is single-factor. Internet exposure is the opposite direction. The hardening is standard privileged-access hygiene: network-restrict the gateway (admin VLAN only), MFA the logons, minimize who can administer the gateway itself, and log everything it does. Convenience tools for admins are high-value targets — harden them proportionally to the access they grant, not the ease they provide.
scenarios.hint: Why must admin tools be hardened proportionally to their access?

scenarios.title: The feature install that failed at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: During an incident, an admin tries to install Telnet Client on a Core server for diagnostics: 'source files not found.' The FoD payload is not cached and there is no local WIM. The incident drags on without the tool.
evidence: Server Core, no GUI, no cached FoD. No WIM on the network share (it was moved).
One diagnostic tool, unavailable when needed most.
choices: Keep installation sources available: maintain a network share with the Windows WIM/FoD payloads, configure Group Policy to point at it (Specify settings for optional component installation), and include source availability in the build checklist. Features install FROM something — that something must exist before the incident. Better: question whether Telnet Client was the right tool (Test-NetConnection is built in), but the systemic fix is source availability
Install every feature preemptively just in case
Telnet Client is deprecated; the admin should know better
Download the feature from the internet during the incident
scenarios.why: Windows features install from a payload — no payload, no feature, no matter how urgent. The 2 AM discovery that the WIM share was moved is a build-hygiene failure, not bad luck. Preemptive installation of everything bloats every server (attack surface, patch load). Scolding the admin about Telnet vs Test-NetConnection is fair but misses the systemic gap (next time it will be a different feature). Internet downloads during an incident depend on internet access from servers (often blocked) and waste incident time. The fix: a maintained, GPO-configured source path for optional components, verified quarterly — part of the build standard, not an afterthought. Incident readiness includes the boring prerequisites.
scenarios.hint: What must exist before you can install a Windows feature on demand?

scenarios.title: The ReFS volume that could not dedup
scenarios.situation: The team formatted the file-share volume as ReFS ('modern and resilient'), then discovered Windows deduplication does not support ReFS the way they planned — the capacity project stalls.
scenarios.prompt: What is the filesystem feature-matrix lesson?
evidence: ReFS, 8TB file share, dedup planned for 40% savings. Reality: dedup support differs by filesystem/version.
Capacity relief this quarter; reformatting means a full data migration.
choices: Check the feature matrix BEFORE formatting: filesystem choice (ReFS vs NTFS) determines available features (dedup, quotas nuances, compression). The fix now: either migrate to NTFS (planned migration window) or achieve capacity another way (quotas, archiving, FSRM reports + cleanup). The lesson is procedural — filesystem selection is a design decision with a checklist (workload, features needed, resiliency), not a default to accept
ReFS is bad; never use it
Dedup is overrated; buy more disks
Convert ReFS to NTFS in place
scenarios.why: ReFS and NTFS are different tools: ReFS brings integrity streams and block cloning (great for virtualization/backup volumes); NTFS brings the mature feature set (dedup, certain quota behaviors). Neither is 'bad' — the error was choosing without consulting the matrix. In-place conversion does not exist (it is a migration). 'Buy more disks' skips the planned savings the project promised. The procedural fix: a filesystem-selection checklist at volume-creation time (workload type → required features → filesystem), reviewed before formatting. For now: pick the least-painful path (planned NTFS migration with dedup, or aggressive quota/cleanup on ReFS) and document the decision. Formatting is a one-way door — decide at the door, not after.
scenarios.hint: Why is filesystem choice a design decision, not a default?

domains.name: Backup & Disaster Recovery
domains.summary: Windows Server Backup, bare-metal recovery, AD forest recovery, and restore testing.

scenarios.title: The backup with no boot media
scenarios.situation: SRV-FILE died completely (motherboard). Good news: full server backups exist on the NAS. Bad news: no recovery boot media was ever created, and the Windows install ISO is three versions behind the server's build.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the recovery plan?
evidence: Full server, current, on NAS — verified present.
No WinRE USB, no current ISO. The 3-versions-old ISO may not restore the newer backup (driver/build mismatch).
choices: Bootable recovery media, maintained: BMR requires booting into recovery environment — without current media, the backups are unreadable when needed most. Fix: create WinRE recovery media per OS version, refresh with each build upgrade, store one copy off-site with the backups. The backup is only half the recovery system; the boot media is the other half
The backups are useless; rebuild from scratch
Download an ISO during the incident; the internet is fast
Restore the backup to a different running server
scenarios.why: Bare-metal recovery is a two-part system: the backup (data) and the boot media (access to the data). Half the system was maintained. A stale ISO risks driver and build incompatibilities at the worst moment; downloading during the incident assumes internet, time, and the right version under pressure. Rebuilding from scratch discards the working backups. Restoring onto a live server is not BMR (and risks the live server). The fix is unglamorous: create recovery media when the server is built, version it with the OS build, store it with (and separately from) the backups, and test-boot it yearly. Recovery media is infrastructure — inventory it like any other.
scenarios.hint: What are the two halves of a bare-metal recovery system?

scenarios.title: The forest recovery nobody rehearsed
scenarios.situation: Tabletop exercise: 'The forest is gone. Walk me through recovery.' The team stares blankly. Nobody has read the AD Forest Recovery Guide. The backup admin says 'we have System State backups' and stops there.
evidence: Backups exist (unverified restores). No customized runbook. Nobody knows the restore order, the authoritative DC choice, or the metadata cleanup steps.
Microsoft's 20+ step forest recovery procedure — unread by the team.
choices: The recovery plan is a hope, not a procedure: forest recovery has strict ordering (isolate, restore forest-root PDC first, seize roles, clean metadata of dead DCs, rebuild the rest, restore trusts) and decisions that must be made BEFORE the disaster (which backup is authoritative? what is the restore order for OUR forest?). The tabletop's value is exposing this NOW: customize the guide to the environment, assign roles, and rehearse yearly. 'We have backups' is step zero of twenty
The backups are sufficient; the guide is overkill
Hire a consultant during the disaster
Forest loss is impossible with two DCs
scenarios.why: System State backups are raw material; forest recovery is the manufacturing process — twenty ordered steps with environment-specific decisions (which DC's backup leads? what is our forest-root? which trusts to restore?). 'We have backups' answers none of them. A consultant during the disaster starts from zero on your environment. 'Impossible' is famous last words (ransomware, admin error, and site loss all kill forests). The tabletop did its job: it converted unknown-unknowns into known gaps while there is time. The deliverable: a customized runbook (forest names filled in, decision criteria written, roles assigned), rehearsed yearly, stored off-site and on paper. Disaster recovery is a practiced skill, not a document.
scenarios.hint: What must be decided about forest recovery BEFORE the disaster?

scenarios.title: The backups that were online
scenarios.situation: Ransomware encrypted all servers AND the backup NAS (it was domain-joined and online). The 'air-gapped' USB rotation was skipped for 6 months ('too much hassle'). The ransom note gives 72 hours.
evidence: NAS online, domain-joined, mapped drives — encrypted with everything else. USB rotation abandoned.
choices: The 3-2-1 rule with true isolation: backups must survive the primary's compromise — that means offline (air-gapped rotation), immutable (WORM/object-lock, undeletable even by admin), or both. A domain-joined online NAS is not a backup target; it is a second copy awaiting encryption. The USB rotation was the isolation layer, and 'hassle' retired it. Rebuild the architecture: immutable cloud/object copies + offline rotation, with restore tested from the isolated copy
Pay the ransom; it is the fastest recovery
The NAS vendor's security failed; sue them
Rebuild everything from scratch without backups
scenarios.why: Ransomware's first target is always the backups — modern strains hunt backup infrastructure explicitly (mapped drives, backup agents, NAS credentials). A domain-joined NAS falls with the domain. The abandoned USB rotation was the only surviving layer, retired for convenience. Paying funds crime, has no guarantee, and marks you as a payer. Lawsuits do not restore data. Rebuilding without data is the business-ending option. The architecture that survives: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 OFFLINE or IMMUTABLE — object-lock/WORM storage that even a compromised admin cannot delete, plus periodic offline copies, with restores TESTED from the isolated copy (an untested air gap is a theory). The hassle of rotation is the price of the guarantee. There is no cheap version of this.
scenarios.hint: Why must one backup copy be offline or immutable?

scenarios.title: The backup that skipped the database
scenarios.situation: The file server backup 'succeeds' nightly, but the accounting database on it is unrestorable — VSS writers have been in 'failed' state for months. The backup captured crash-consistent files, not a valid database.
evidence: vssadmin list writers: SqlServerWriter — Failed, retryable error, for months.
Status Success (files copied); database integrity: unrestorable.
choices: VSS writer health: application-consistent backup requires healthy VSS writers — a failed writer means the app was never quiesced, and the 'backup' is crash-consistent at best. The check is trivial (vssadmin list writers, or the backup software's writer status) and must be part of backup monitoring, with alerts on non-Stable writers. 'Success' without writer health is a file copy, not a database backup. Rebuild the writer state, take a proper backup, and test-restore the database
The database needs its own backup software
File backups are sufficient for databases
Restore the database from the file backup and repair it
scenarios.why: VSS is the contract between the backup and the application: the writer quiesces the app (flush, freeze) so the snapshot is transactionally consistent. A failed writer voids the contract silently — the backup job still 'succeeds' because files were copied. Crash-consistent database files are not a database backup; they are a recovery project with uncertain outcome. Separate backup software does not fix an unwatched writer. Repairing a crash-consistent DB is hope-based recovery. The operational fix: VSS writer health is a monitored metric (alert on anything but Stable, investigate retryable errors promptly), and database restores are test-restored on schedule. The backup report should include writer state — green writers, green backup, or it is not green.
scenarios.hint: What does a failed VSS writer mean for the backup's usability?

scenarios.title: The recovery with no order
scenarios.situation: Site power event: 40 servers down. Recovery begins — with the print server, because its admin shouted loudest. Three hours later, nobody can log on (DCs still down) and the ticket system (also down) cannot track anything.
evidence: Ad-hoc order by volume of shouting. Identity (DCs/DNS) still down at hour 3.
Everything depends on AD/DNS; the ticket system depends on the DB; nobody mapped this.
choices: A recovery priority order based on dependencies: Tier 0 — identity and network (DCs, DNS, DHCP); Tier 1 — backup/monitoring/management; Tier 2 — data and applications by business priority (ticket system before print). The order is decided in calm planning, written down, and followed under pressure — because pressure produces print-server-first. Publish the tiers, assign owners, rehearse the sequence
Recover everything simultaneously; it is faster
The loudest admin had a point; printing matters
Buy generators so this never happens again
scenarios.why: Recovery without priorities is recovery by politics: the loudest voice wins, dependencies lose. Identity-first is not a preference — it is physics: nothing authenticates, resolves names, or gets addresses until Tier 0 is up, so every 'recovered' app server before that is theater. Simultaneous recovery of 40 servers is resource contention (network, storage, admin attention) with no sequencing. Generators address power, not the next flood/fire/ransomware. The deliverable: a written, dependency-ordered recovery sequence with tier definitions, business-priority input (the business ranks Tier 2, IT ranks Tier 0/1), named owners per tier, and a rehearsal record. In the disaster, the plan — not the shouting — sets the order.
scenarios.hint: What is the correct recovery tier order, and why?

scenarios.title: The retention that kept everything
scenarios.situation: Backup retention: 'keep everything forever.' The NAS is 95% full of 4-year-old incrementals. The backup job now fails nightly (no space). Finance asks why storage costs tripled.
evidence: No retention policy — infinite retention by default. 4 years of incrementals, mostly unrestorable as chains (missing fulls pruned by space pressure).
Actual requirements: 30 daily, 12 monthly, 7 yearly (finance/compliance) — never written down.
choices: A defined retention policy matched to real requirements: GFS-style (grandfather-father-son: dailies 30d, weeklies/monthlies 12m, yearlies 7y per compliance), enforced automatically, with the oldest pruned as new arrive. 'Keep everything' is not a policy — it is the absence of one, and it fails in the most expensive way (storage costs triple, jobs fail, old chains are unrestorable anyway). Write the policy from compliance + business needs, automate enforcement, review yearly
Buy more NAS
Delete the oldest backups manually each month
Keep everything; storage is cheap
scenarios.why: Infinite retention has three costs: money (tripled storage), reliability (jobs fail when full — the backup system breaks itself), and false confidence (4-year incremental chains with pruned fulls are unrestorable — kept but useless). Manual monthly deletion is toil that gets skipped (how the 4 years accumulated). 'Storage is cheap' ignores that unmanaged growth is unbounded. The professional answer: retention derived from requirements (compliance mandates, business RPO/RTO, legal hold) expressed as a tiered policy, enforced by the backup software automatically, with capacity planning against the policy's steady state. The policy is a document with an owner and a review date — because requirements change, and 'forever' is never the answer.
scenarios.hint: How do you derive a backup retention policy?

scenarios.title: The restore test that never happened
scenarios.situation: The file server's data is needed after a RAID failure. The backups are 'green.' The restore fails: the backup agent's encryption key was changed 8 months ago and the old key — needed for the older full — is lost. The chain is unreadable.
evidence: Encrypted, key rotated 8 months ago, old key not archived. Full backup from 9 months ago needs the old key.
Green backups, unreadable chain. Data effectively lost.
choices: Encryption key lifecycle management: backup encryption keys must be archived with the backups they protect, for the full retention period — key rotation without key archiving destroys old backups. The key inventory (which key decrypts which backup era) is part of the backup system, stored separately from the backups, with its own backup. And the restore test that would have caught this 8 months ago was never run
Do not encrypt backups; encryption causes this
The backup software should manage keys automatically
Rotate keys more often to limit exposure
scenarios.why: Encrypted backups are only as recoverable as their keys: rotating the key without archiving the old one is key destruction with extra steps — every backup from the old era becomes cryptographic noise. 'Do not encrypt' trades a key-management problem for a data-exposure problem (unencrypted backups of payroll data on a NAS). Software key management helps only if it archives across rotation (verify, do not assume). More frequent rotation multiplies the key inventory without fixing archiving. The system: keys archived per era, inventory mapping eras to keys, keys backed up separately (not with the data they protect — the fire takes both), and restore tests that actually DECRYPT old-era backups. The 8-month-old gap is the real indictment — a single old-backup restore test would have found it.
scenarios.hint: Why must old backup encryption keys be archived?

lessons.title: Windows Systems Administration — Core concepts
concepts: Core administration: services.msc controls service state and startup type; the Registry holds system configuration; Event Viewer (System, Application, Security logs) is the causal record — control first, cause second, fix third.
NTFS vs share permissions: effective access is the most restrictive of the two layers; enforce policy at the NTFS layer and keep shares simple.
Active Directory: forests contain trees of domains; OUs organize objects for Group Policy, which applies in LSDOU order (Local, Site, Domain, OU — closest link wins).
Authentication: Kerberos is the default domain protocol (ticket-based, needs correct SPNs); NTLM is the legacy fallback — its appearance in logs signals a misconfiguration to investigate.
PowerShell: the pipeline passes objects with properties — Get-VerbNoun cmdlets retrieve, Where-Object filters, Select-Object shapes output.
Windows networking: DNS resolves names (watch the client cache), DHCP assigns addresses and options; file/print services and Remote Desktop/Remote Access complete the server's network role set.

example.code:
# Audit: find every running service whose name starts with SQL,
# show name and status, export to CSV for the change ticket
Get-Service |
    Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' -and $_.Name -like 'SQL*' } |
    Select-Object Name, Status, StartType |
    Export-Csv C:\audit\sql-services.csv -NoTypeInformation
# Verify the file landed:
Get-Item C:\audit\sql-services.csv | Select-Object Length, LastWriteTime
example.walkthrough: This is the get → filter → shape pattern in one pipeline: Get-Service emits service objects, Where-Object keeps only running ones matching 'SQL*', Select-Object projects three properties, and Export-Csv persists the evidence. The final Get-Item confirms the artifact exists — the habit of verifying output is what separates a script from a hope.

pitfalls: Common trap: restarting a failed service without checking Event Viewer — you treated the symptom and the failure will recur.
Common trap: opening share permissions instead of fixing NTFS — the most restrictive layer wins, so broad shares plus tight NTFS is the correct posture.
Common trap: unlinking a Group Policy to fix one user's problem — policy is OU-scoped; fix the object or the setting, not the whole policy.
Common trap: treating NTLM in the logs as normal — its presence usually means Kerberos broke down (bad or duplicate SPN), and that deserves investigation.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Windows Admin move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Windows Systems Administration
concepts: Windows Systems Administration is a multi-step process within Windows Systems Administration: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Windows Systems Administration to the broader Windows Systems Administration ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Windows Systems Administration begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Windows Systems Administration. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Windows Systems Administration as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Windows Systems Administration flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: Start Here: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: Three content types: lessons (concepts with worked examples), scenarios (timed decision drills — read the evidence before choosing), and labs (hands-on exercises with command checks).
Work each domain as a triad: lessons first, then scenarios closed-book, then labs. The triad converts reading into doing.
Mock Assessment is your final exam — it draws from every domain at runtime. Attempt it only when every domain is green.
Systems Anatomy is shared fundamentals (OS and networking concepts every Windows admin needs). Interviews probe these basics mercilessly — do not skip it.

example.code:

Reasoning: Load the model, test recall under pressure, prove with commands.
Takeaway: One triad pass per domain beats three passive re-reads.
example.walkthrough: Run one full triad on the Active Directory domain today; log your three weakest topics.

pitfalls: Jumping to scenarios without lessons — the 'why' explanations assume lesson vocabulary.
Skipping labs: Windows administration is a doing discipline; interviewers spot theory-only candidates fast.
Taking the mock first 'for a baseline' — it wastes your only dress rehearsal.
