lessons.title: Study Strategy: The Windows Admin Learning Loop
concepts: Learn in three layers: Layer 1 — the mental model (what AD replication does, how GPO processing orders). Layer 2 — the tool for each job (which console, which PowerShell cmdlet). Layer 3 — failure modes (the FSMO holder dies, SYSVOL stops replicating).
For every lesson ask 'what breaks if this is misconfigured?' Admin interviews are 70% failure-mode questions.
Build a personal runbook: every lab's commands, copied verbatim. It becomes your incident-response cheat sheet.
Revisit scenarios 48 hours after passing them. GPO precedence (LSDOU) and NTFS-vs-share effective access are the classic fade-fast details.

example.code:
Worked example — the failure-mode habit
Setup: Lesson teaches DHCP failover.
Reasoning: Ask: 'What happens when the partner goes down? What if the scope is full?'
Takeaway: Three self-asked failure questions per lesson build interview answers.
example.walkthrough: After each lesson, write three 'what breaks if...' questions and answer from memory.

pitfalls: Memorizing console names without the underlying model — consoles change, concepts do not.
Studying domains in isolation: real incidents chain them (DNS breaks AD breaks GPO).
No runbook: knowledge you cannot type at 3 AM is trivia.
lessons.try_it: Start your runbook file: one section per domain, commands only.

lessons.title: What Interviews and Exams Actually Test
concepts: Interviewers test five things: Active Directory fluency (OUs, GPOs, Kerberos, FSMO), PowerShell automation (pipeline thinking, remoting), DNS/DHCP troubleshooting methodology, Hyper-V and storage fundamentals, and backup/recovery credibility.
Expect scenario questions: 'Users cannot log on — walk me through it.' Answers must show a methodology (check scope, DNS, AD, GPO — in order) with concrete tools named.

Exam-style questions weight: GPO processing order and precedence, NTFS vs share effective permissions, FSMO roles and seizure, DNS record types, DHCP DORA process, and PowerShell verb-noun pipeline semantics.
The differentiator: recovery stories. 'I seized the PDC emulator after a host failure' beats any definition. The capstone gives you real stories.

example.code:
Worked example — answering 'users cannot log on'
Setup: Monday 9 AM, helpdesk flooded.
Reasoning: Wrong: 'reboot the DC.' Right: scope (all users? one site?), check DNS (can clients resolve the DC?), check DC health (Netlogon, SYSVOL), check GPO/recent change.
Takeaway: Methodology with named tools beats heroic guessing.
example.walkthrough: Answer three scenarios aloud in 90 seconds each, whiteboard style.

pitfalls: Reciting definitions instead of demonstrating methodology.
Skipping DNS in every troubleshooting answer — AD without DNS is down by definition.
No recovery experience: build the capstone so you have true stories.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself troubleshooting one scenario; check for named tools.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: From Core OS to Production Infrastructure
concepts: Phase 1 — Core: server-roles, file-services, dns-dhcp. Goal: install, configure, and troubleshoot a standalone Windows Server.
Phase 2 — Identity: active-directory, group-policy. Goal: build a domain, join machines, deploy policy that actually applies.
Phase 3 — Automation & virtualization: powershell, hyper-v. Goal: script routine tasks, virtualize workloads properly.
Phase 4 — Production: patching-wsus, monitoring, backup-dr. Goal: keep it patched, watched, and recoverable. Capstone ties all four phases into one environment.
Pace: one phase per week, one triad per day. The capstone is your portfolio proof — build it for real in a lab, not on paper.

example.code:
Worked example — phase gate
Setup: End of Phase 2.
Reasoning: Gate: build a domain, create an OU structure, link a GPO, prove it applies with gpresult.
Takeaway: Gates are provable skills, not chapters finished.
example.walkthrough: Write your four phase-gate checklists now.

pitfalls: Skipping phases: Phase 2 assumes Phase 1 DNS skills — AD install fails without them.
No capstone: 'I know Windows Server' without a built environment is unverifiable.
Rushing: a shaky Phase 1 makes every later phase painful.
lessons.try_it: Schedule your phase gates on the calendar this week.

lessons.title: Capstone Brief: Build a Production-Like Windows Environment
concepts: Your capstone: a virtualized lab with two domain controllers (DNS + DHCP failover), a file server (DFS namespace), a Hyper-V host, WSUS, centralized event collection, and a backup server — all on Server Core where possible, all configured via PowerShell.

Constraints that make it real: no GUI crutches on the servers (RSAT from your workstation), every setting scripted and in git, GPOs documented with purpose, and a service account/permission model following least privilege.
Deliverables: network diagram, all PowerShell as files, GPO documentation, a runbook (DC failure, ransomware restore, bad patch rollback), and a demo walkthrough.
Grading: kill a DC — does logon still work? Restore a file from backup — how long? Roll back a bad update — what is the procedure?

example.code:
Worked example — the demo narrative
Setup: 'Show me patching.'
Reasoning: WSUS approves to pilot group → GPO installs Sunday 2 AM → monitoring confirms → report shows compliance.
Takeaway: The demo tells the production story end to end.
example.walkthrough: Write your capstone brief: components, constraints, survival tests.

pitfalls: Building everything with the mouse: unrepeatable, undocumented, unhirable.
Single DC 'to keep it simple': you cannot demo any failure scenario.
No runbook: the documentation is half the deliverable.
lessons.try_it: Create the repo and commit the network diagram today.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: Identity, Network, and Data
concepts: Identity: one forest, one domain (lab.local), two DCs (PDC + partner), OU design by function (Workstations, Servers, Service Accounts), GPOs linked at OU level — never at the domain root unless truly global.
Network: DNS AD-integrated on both DCs, DHCP failover pair, Hyper-V virtual switches (external/management separation), NIC teaming on the host.
Data: file server with DFS namespace (\\lab.local\shares), NTFS least-privilege + simple shares, quotas via FSRM, Windows Server Backup to dedicated disk.
Operations: WSUS downstream of nothing (standalone), Event Forwarding to a collector, Performance baselines captured at build time for later comparison.

example.code:
Worked example — the OU decision
Setup: Where does the WSUS GPO link?
Reasoning: Pilot OU gets pilot policy; Production OU gets production policy; Servers OU separate. Domain-root linking avoided.
Takeaway: OU design IS policy design.
example.walkthrough: Draw the full architecture: every server, role, OU, and GPO link.

pitfalls: Flat AD (everything in default containers): GPO targeting becomes impossible.
DHCP on one DC only: a reboot takes down address assignment.
No baseline: later 'it is slow' has nothing to compare against.
lessons.try_it: Write the OU/GPO design document with justification per link.

lessons.title: Capstone Verification: Proving It Works
concepts: Verification suite: (1) shut down DC1 — logon and DNS still work via DC2; (2) delete a file — restore from backup, timed; (3) approve a bad update to pilot — roll back per procedure; (4) seize a FSMO role in lab and transfer it back.
Negative tests: break a GPO (bad setting) and show the troubleshooting path (gpresult, event log); fill a DHCP scope and show the alert fires.
Evidence: screenshots of dcdiag clean, repadmin /showrepl healthy, backup success logs, WSUS compliance report. These are portfolio artifacts.
Script the verifications. A runbook nobody can re-run is fiction — and interviewers ask 'how did you test it?'

Worked example — the DC failure test
Setup: DC1 powered off.
Reasoning: Client logon → DNS resolves via DC2 → dcdiag on DC2 clean → power DC1 back, replication converges.
Takeaway: One executed failure test beats ten architecture slides.
example.walkthrough: Script and run your four verification tests; save the evidence.

pitfalls: Happy-path only: interviewers ask 'what did you break on purpose?'
Manual-only verification: unrepeatable means unverifiable.
No evidence captured: the portfolio needs the screenshots, not your memory.

lessons.title: Windows Services Deep Dive
concepts: Services run in sessions with identities: LocalSystem (god-mode, no network creds), NetworkService (machine creds), LocalService (limited), or a gMSA/service account (least privilege, managed password).
Recovery actions: first/second/subsequent failure can restart, run a program, or reboot. Configure them — a service that dies silently at 3 AM is a monitoring failure.
Dependencies: services start in dependency order; a delayed-start dependency (e.g., SQL waiting on storage) explains 'starts manually but not at boot.'
Troubleshoot path: services.msc state → Event Log (Service Control Manager, event 7000/7001/7034) → service-specific log → dependency chain → account password expired?

example.code:
sc.exe failure MyService reset=86400 actions=restart/60000/restart/60000/reboot/60000
# first two failures: restart after 60s; third: reboot the box
example.walkthrough: Configure recovery actions on a lab service; kill it and watch the recovery fire.

pitfalls: Running everything as LocalSystem: a compromised service owns the box AND cannot be audited per-service.
Automatic startup for a service needing manual prerequisites: boot-time failures that 'work when I start it.'
Ignoring 7009 timeouts: 'service did not respond in 30000ms' usually means a dependency was not ready.
lessons.try_it: Audit every Automatic service's logon account; convert to gMSA where possible.

lessons.title: The Registry: Configuration Database
concepts: The registry is a hierarchical config database: HKLM (machine), HKCU (user), HKCR (file associations), HKU, HKCC. Services, drivers, and apps read it at start — and often only at start.
Back it up before touching it: reg export, System Restore points, or full backup. There is no undo and no recycle bin.
Common admin paths: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services (service config), \Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (startup), Policies keys (GPO registry settings land here).
Prefer Group Policy Preferences over raw registry edits for fleet changes: auditable, reversible, targeted — regedit is for diagnosis and one-offs.

example.code:
reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\w32time /v Start
# 2 = Automatic, 3 = Manual, 4 = Disabled
example.walkthrough: Export a service key, change its Start value in lab, reboot, observe, restore.

pitfalls: Editing the registry on a hunch: always export first, and know the restore command before the edit.
HKLM edits expecting instant effect: most services read config at start — restart the service.
Scripting reg add across the fleet: use GPO Preferences instead for targeting and rollback.
lessons.try_it: Document the five registry paths you touch most; add export commands to the runbook.

lessons.title: Task Scheduler: Automation Without Agents
concepts: Task Scheduler runs jobs on triggers (schedule, event, logon, idle) as chosen principals — including SYSTEM and gMSAs — with conditions (AC power, network) and history per task.
Security: tasks store credentials; 'run whether user is logged on or not' with a stored password is a credential to protect. Prefer gMSA principals (no stored password).
Reliability: set 'stop if runs longer than', retry on failure, and alert on Last Run Result != 0. A scheduled task nobody monitors is a silent failure generator.
PowerShell + Scheduled Tasks is the poor man's orchestrator: log rotation, report generation, health checks — all without extra agents.

example.code: schtasks /create /tn "NightlyBackupCheck" /tr "powershell.exe -File C:\Scripts\Check-Backup.ps1" /sc daily /st 02:00 /ru "SYSTEM"
example.walkthrough: Create a scheduled health-check task writing to the event log; verify history shows success.

pitfalls: Tasks as Administrator with stored passwords: password changes break them silently months later.
No failure alerting: the task failed for 6 months and nobody knew.
Overlapping schedules: long-running tasks stacking up — set execution time limits.
lessons.try_it: Inventory all scheduled tasks on one server; document owner and purpose per task.

lessons.title: Windows Networking Fundamentals for Admins
concepts: The admin's network stack: IP config (Get-NetIPConfiguration), DNS client cache (DisplayDns/Clear-DnsClientCache), routing table (Get-NetRoute), firewall (Get-NetFirewallRule), and SMB shares.
Name resolution order matters: hosts file → DNS cache → DNS server. A stale hosts entry or poisoned cache beats correct DNS every time.
Windows Firewall with Advanced Security is host-based segmentation: default inbound block, rule-based allows. It is part of every server's security posture — not optional.
Test-NetConnection is the Swiss army knife: ping, TCP port test, traceroute in one cmdlet. Use it before blaming the application.

example.code:
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName dc01.lab.local -Port 389
# proves name resolution AND LDAP reachability in one call
example.walkthrough: Diagnose a 'cannot reach server' ticket using only Test-NetConnection and DNS cache commands.

pitfalls: Disabling the firewall 'to fix' connectivity: you removed the symptom and the protection.
Forgetting the DNS client cache: ipconfig /flushdns fixes the 'DNS is wrong but the server is right' ticket.
Testing with ping only: ping proves ICMP, not that port 389/636/3268 is open.
lessons.try_it: Write the 5-command network triage sequence into your runbook.

lessons.title: Remote Management: WinRM and RSAT
concepts: WinRM is Windows' remote management transport (WS-Management): PowerShell remoting, Server Manager, and many MMCs ride it. Enable-PSRemoting configures the listener and firewall rule.
RSAT on your workstation + Server Core on servers is the professional pattern: full GUI tools locally, minimal attack surface remotely.

Remoting security: Kerberos in-domain (no credential exposure), CredSSP only when double-hop is unavoidable (and understand its credential-delegation risk), Just Enough Administration (JEA) for constrained delegation.
Double-hop problem: your credential cannot hop from ServerA to ServerB by default — that is a security feature. Solutions: CredSSP (risky), Kerberos delegation (scoped), or JEA endpoints (best).

example.walkthrough: Enable remoting on two lab servers; run a one-to-many Invoke-Command.

pitfalls: CredSSP everywhere 'because it works': it delegates your full credential — scope it or avoid it.
WinRM over HTTP without Kerberos: credentials in the clear on untrusted networks — use HTTPS listeners there.
RDP for everything: RDP is interactive and heavy; remoting is scriptable and auditable.
lessons.try_it: Convert one RDP-based routine task to a remoting one-liner this week.

lessons.title: Reading Performance Counters Like an Admin
concepts: The four resources: CPU (% Processor Time, queue length), memory (Available MB, page faults/sec), disk (Avg. Disk sec/Read-Write, queue length), network (output queue). Bottlenecks show in exactly one place first.
Methodology: establish baseline when healthy, compare under complaint. 'Slow' without a baseline is an opinion; with counters it is a diagnosis.
Common misreads: high CPU % with low queue = busy but coping; sustained queue > 2 per core = real CPU pressure. Memory pressure shows as hard page faults + disk activity, not just 'low available MB.'
PAL-style thinking: capture with Performance Monitor (Data Collector Sets), analyze offline, keep the baselines with the server's documentation.

example.code:
Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time' -SampleInterval 2 -MaxSamples 5
Get-Counter '\Memory\Available MBytes', '\LogicalDisk(C:)\Avg. Disk sec/Read'
example.walkthrough: Baseline a lab server at idle and under load; save both captures.

pitfalls: Chasing the wrong resource: 'slow server' blamed on CPU when disk latency is 200ms.
One snapshot instead of a trend: counters lie in single samples — sample over time.
No baseline: every investigation starts from zero.
lessons.try_it: Create baselines for your capstone servers at build time.

lessons.title: TCP/IP Troubleshooting on Windows
concepts: The stack, bottom-up: physical link (Get-NetAdapter status) → IP config (address, mask, gateway) → DNS resolution → TCP connectivity (port) → application. Test in order; the first failure is the layer to fix.
APIPA (169.254.x.x) means DHCP failed — the address itself is the diagnosis. Duplicate IP warnings in the event log mean exactly what they say.
Tools per layer: ping (basic reachability), Test-NetConnection (port), Resolve-DnsName (DNS), Get-NetRoute (routing), Get-NetTCPConnection (what is listening).
Remember: Windows prefers IPv6; a broken IPv6 path with working IPv4 causes bizarre intermittent failures. Check both, or scope v6 deliberately.

example.code:
Resolve-DnsName dc01.lab.local
Test-NetConnection dc01.lab.local -Port 389
Get-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix '0.0.0.0/0'
example.walkthrough: Break networking in lab (wrong gateway) and diagnose layer by layer.

pitfalls: Starting at the application layer: hours wasted before checking the cable/config.
Ignoring IPv6: 'sometimes works' is the signature of a v6/v4 split.
Flushing DNS for a routing problem: match the tool to the layer.
lessons.try_it: Write the bottom-up triage checklist; laminate it mentally.

lessons.title: AD DS Core: Forests, Domains, and Trusts
concepts: A forest is the security boundary: one schema, one configuration partition, shared global catalog. Domains partition replication and policy. Trees share a contiguous namespace; forests are separate namespaces joined by trust.
Trusts: transitive two-way within a forest automatically; forest trusts are explicit. Trust direction matters: A trusts B means B's users access A's resources.
Global Catalog: partial attribute set of every object in the forest, on GC servers — logon and forest-wide searches need it. Every site should have one.
Design rule: single forest, single domain unless you have a hard reason (regulatory, acquisition). Complexity is a cost paid forever.

example.code:
Get-ADForest | Select Name, Domains
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select Name, Direction, TrustType
example.walkthrough: Map your lab forest: domains, trusts, GC placement.

pitfalls: Multi-domain 'for security': domains are NOT security boundaries — the forest is.
No GC in a remote site: logons crawl across the WAN.
Trusts without documentation: nobody knows why DomainB can reach the file server.
lessons.try_it: Document your forest design with the reason for each domain.

lessons.title: OUs, Delegation, and the Admin Tier Model
concepts: OUs organize objects for Group Policy and delegation — design by administration need (Workstations, Servers, Service Accounts), not by org chart (org charts change).
Delegation: grant granular rights at the OU (reset passwords, join computers) without Domain Admin. The Delegation of Control Wizard creates auditable, least-privilege grants.
Tier model: Tier 0 (DCs, AD itself — only hardened admin workstations), Tier 1 (servers), Tier 2 (workstations). Credentials never flow upward: no Tier 2 admin logging into Tier 0.
Protected Users and Authentication Policies: modern hardening for privileged accounts (no NTLM, no delegation, short Kerberos lifetimes).

example.code:
dsacls 'OU=Workstations,DC=lab,DC=local'
# review who can do what before delegating more
example.walkthrough: Design your OU tree; delegate password-reset to helpdesk at one OU.

pitfalls: Flat default containers: GPOs cannot target, delegation is all-or-nothing.
Domain Admins for daily work: every workstation compromise becomes a forest compromise.
Tier violations: RDPing from a workstation to a DC with a DA account.
lessons.try_it: Implement tiering: separate accounts for workstation vs server vs DC admin.

lessons.title: Kerberos: How Domain Authentication Really Works
concepts: Kerberos flow: client → KDC (AS-REQ) gets TGT → TGS-REQ for a service gets service ticket → presents ticket to the server. No passwords cross the wire after initial logon.
SPNs (Service Principal Names) map services to accounts: a duplicate or missing SPN breaks Kerberos and falls back to NTLM — NTLM in the logs is a symptom to investigate, not normal.
Time sync is authentication: >5 min skew breaks Kerberos. The PDC emulator is the domain time source; clients sync from DCs. 'Random logon failures' — check time first.
Delegation (unconstrained/constrained/RBCD): lets a service act as the user to a backend. Unconstrained delegation is a credential-theft amplifier — use constrained or resource-based instead.

example.code:
setspn -Q HTTP/web01.lab.local
# duplicate SPNs break Kerberos; this query finds them
example.walkthrough: Find duplicate SPNs in lab; fix one and watch NTLM log entries drop.

pitfalls: Ignoring NTLM fallback: it signals SPN/time/config problems.
Unconstrained delegation 'because the app needs it': compromise the front end, harvest every user's TGT.
Time drift: the silent killer of Monday-morning logons.
lessons.try_it: Audit delegation settings on all service accounts quarterly.

lessons.title: FSMO Roles: What They Are and When They Break
concepts: Five roles: Schema Master, Domain Naming Master (forest), RID Master, PDC Emulator, Infrastructure Master (domain). Single-master operations that cannot be multi-mastered safely.
PDC Emulator is the busy one: time source, password-change authority, GPO editor default. Its loss is felt immediately; the others can be down for days unnoticed.
Transfer (graceful, online) vs seize (forceful, old holder must NEVER return). Seizure is for dead holders only — a seized-then-returned DC corrupts the directory.
Know the holders: netdom query fsmo. Document them. Monitor them. The 3 AM call is always the role nobody documented.

example.code:
netdom query fsmo
Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterIdentity -Identity DC02 -OperationMasterRole PDCEmulator
example.walkthrough: Transfer the PDC role in lab; seize it back after 'killing' the holder; verify.

pitfalls: Seizing a role from a live DC: never do this — transfer instead.
All FSMO on one DC 'for simplicity': one failure takes all five.
Seized holder reconnected: it must be wiped and rebuilt, never rejoined.
lessons.try_it: Document FSMO placement and the seizure procedure in the runbook.

lessons.title: AD Backup and Authoritative Restore
concepts: System State backup on DCs captures AD (ntds.dit), SYSVOL, registry. Back up at least two DCs per domain — one backup is a single point of failure.

Non-authoritative restore: DC rebuilt from backup, then replicates IN the changes since — normal case. Authoritative: restored objects replicate OUT, overwriting the domain — for accidental mass deletion.
Forest recovery is a defined procedure (Microsoft's AD Forest Recovery Guide): isolate, restore, seize, clean metadata, rebuild. Read it BEFORE the disaster; it is a 20+ step procedure.
Tombstone/recycle bin: AD Recycle Bin (enabled deliberately, forest-wide) makes single-object recovery trivial — enable it on day one. It cannot be disabled after.

example.code:
wbadmin start systemstatebackup -backuptarget:E:
# then: verify with wbadmin get versions
example.walkthrough: Enable the AD Recycle Bin in lab; delete and restore an OU.

pitfalls: No System State backups: 'we back up the VM' — VM snapshots of DCs cause USN rollback; use supported methods.
Authoritative restore for a non-authoritative problem: you just replicated old data over good data.
Recycle Bin never enabled: every deleted object is a backup-restore exercise.
lessons.try_it: Verify System State backups exist for two DCs; test one restore.

lessons.title: GPO Processing: LSDOU and Precedence
concepts: Processing order: Local, Site, Domain, OU (LSDOU) — later wins on conflict. Within an OU chain, the closest linked GPO wins. Enforced overrides Block Inheritance; Block stops inheritance unless Enforced.
Link order within a container: lower number = higher precedence (processed last). Link order 1 beats link order 2.
Enforced is the sledgehammer: it wins over everything below AND cannot be blocked. Use sparingly — every Enforced GPO is a future troubleshooting mystery.
Computer vs User: computer settings apply at startup, user at logon. A user setting in a computer-targeted OU does nothing without loopback.

example.code:
gpresult /r
# shows applied GPOs in precedence order — the fastest precedence check
example.walkthrough: Create two conflicting GPOs at different levels; predict the winner with gpresult.

pitfalls: Enforced everywhere: precedence becomes unreadable and Block Inheritance stops working.
Domain-root linking for OU-specific needs: every computer pays the processing cost.
Forgetting link order: 'but my GPO is linked!' — at what order?
lessons.try_it: Document the GPO precedence map for your domain.

lessons.title: Security Policies and Templates
concepts: Security Settings node: account policies (password, lockout, Kerberos), local policies (user rights, audit), firewall, software restriction/AppLocker. The hardening toolkit.
Baselines: Microsoft Security Baselines (downloadable GPO backups) give a vetted starting point — import, compare, adapt. Do not hand-roll hardening from memory.
User Rights Assignment is powerful and dangerous: 'Deny log on locally' for service accounts, 'Log on as a service' scoped tightly. Test on pilot OUs — a bad rights GPO locks out admins.
Audit policy via GPO (Advanced Audit Policy): logon events, object access, policy change. Tune before enabling broadly — noisy auditing fills disks and hides signal.

example.code:
auditpol /get /category:* 
# shows effective advanced audit policy — compare against the GPO intent
example.walkthrough: Import a security baseline to a pilot OU; compare its settings to your current GPOs.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled hardening with no baseline: inconsistent and unauditable.
Deny rights applied too broadly: the classic self-lockout (test on pilot!).
Full auditing with no log management: disks fill, the 'security' becomes an outage.
lessons.try_it: Pilot every security GPO change; keep a rollback GPO ready.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting GPOs: gpresult and Event Logs
concepts: Methodology: (1) scope — does the GPO apply to this object? (gpresult /r, /h report) (2) replication — did the DCs converge? (repadmin, SYSVOL) (3) client — did it process? (event log, gpupdate /force).
gpresult /h report.html is the single best tool: applied vs denied GPOs with reasons (empty WMI filter, security filtering, blocked inheritance). Read the 'denied' section first.
Event IDs: 1058/1030 (SYSVOL/GPO access — usually DNS or permissions), 1085/1096 (processing failures). Group Policy Operational log has the detail.
Replication gotchas: GPO = AD object (version) + SYSVOL files (content). Version mismatch between them = 'GPO not applying' with no clear error. Check both.

example.code:
gpresult /h C:\temp\gpo.html
# open it: Applied GPOs, then 'Denied GPOs' with reasons
example.walkthrough: Break a GPO in lab (security filtering); diagnose using only gpresult.

pitfalls: gpupdate /force as the first step: it masks replication problems temporarily.
Checking only one DC: the client may use another DC with stale SYSVOL.
Ignoring the Denied section: the answer is usually written there.
lessons.try_it: Write the 3-step GPO triage into the runbook.

lessons.title: Preferences vs Policies
concepts: Policies (Administrative Templates): enforced, registry-backed, tattooed while applied and REMOVED when unlinked (most). True policy — user cannot override.

Preferences: deploy settings (drive maps, printers, registry, files, shortcuts) with targeting (item-level targeting: apply only to laptop users in Finance). Flexible, but users CAN change them (reapplied at refresh).
Rule of thumb: enforce with Policies, deploy with Preferences. Drive mappings and printer deployment are Preferences' home turf.
Preferences passwords are forbidden: the old cpasswords vulnerability (AES key published) means any 'password' in a preference XML is retrievable by any domain user. Never store secrets in GPP.

example.code:
# preferences deploy a drive map with targeting — configured in GPMC, not code
# verify: gpresult shows it under 'Applied Group Policy Objects' -> Preferences
example.walkthrough: Deploy a mapped drive via Preferences with item-level targeting to one security group.

pitfalls: Storing passwords in Preferences: retrievable by ANY authenticated user — use LAPS/gMSA instead.
Using Preferences where enforcement is needed: users change it, refresh may not reapply for hours.
No targeting: the printer deploys to the entire domain.
lessons.try_it: Search all GPP XMLs for cpassword remnants; remediate any found.

lessons.title: Loopback Processing and Security Filtering
concepts: Loopback: when USER settings must follow the COMPUTER (kiosk, lab, terminal server). Merge mode (user's GPOs + computer's user-settings) vs Replace (only the computer's).
Classic use: locked-down lab computers where any user logging on gets the lab policy regardless of their own OU. Replace mode is the kiosk answer.

Security filtering: scope a GPO to a group instead of 'Authenticated Users' — but remember the computer needs READ access too (or 'Authenticated Users' read + group apply). The 2016+ default requires care here.
WMI filters: target by OS, hardware, etc. Powerful but slow — each filter evaluates at every refresh. Keep them simple or replace with group targeting.

example.code:
# loopback set on the computer OU's GPO:
# Computer Config > Policies > Admin Templates > System > Group Policy > User Group Policy loopback processing mode
example.walkthrough: Build a kiosk OU with loopback Replace; verify a domain admin logging on gets locked down.

pitfalls: Loopback in Merge when Replace was needed: the user's own policies leak through.
Security filtering removing Authenticated Users entirely: computers cannot read the GPO — nothing applies.
Complex WMI filters: logon times balloon; users blame the network.
lessons.try_it: Document every loopback and filtered GPO with its reason.

lessons.title: Windows DNS: Zones and Records
concepts: Zone types: primary/secondary (legacy file), stub, and AD-integrated (recommended — replication via AD, secure dynamic updates, multi-master). AD-integrated is the default choice in a domain.
Records you must know cold: A/AAAA (host), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), SRV (service location — AD lives on SRV records), PTR (reverse), NS/SOA (delegation).
AD DEPENDS on DNS: DC locator SRV records (_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs) are how clients find DCs. DNS broken = AD broken = logon broken. DNS is always step one in AD troubleshooting.

Aging/scavenging: cleans stale dynamic records. Configure it (or watch the zone fill with ghost records of dead machines) — but set no-refresh + refresh intervals sanely to avoid deleting live records.

example.code:
Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.local
# no answer = clients cannot find a DC = logons fail
example.walkthrough: Verify the _msdcs SRV records exist; delete one in lab and watch logon break.

pitfalls: Non-AD-integrated primary on one server: single point of failure for name resolution.
Scavenging misconfigured: live records vanish, 'random' outages follow.
External forwarders only, no root hints plan: understand the resolution path you built.
lessons.try_it: Confirm every DC runs AD-integrated DNS; document forwarder design.

lessons.title: DNS Troubleshooting Methodology
concepts: Order: client cache → client config (right DNS server?) → server (is the record there?) → zone/replication → forwarders/root hints. The first failure is the fix layer.
Tools: Resolve-DnsName (with -Server to test specific servers), nslookup (interactive), dnscmd /zoneinfo, DNS debug logging (server-side, verbose — enable briefly).
Classic: 'works with IP, fails with name' = name resolution, period. 'Fails for one client' = client-side (cache/hosts/config). 'Fails for all' = server/zone.
Negative caching: failed lookups are cached too. After fixing DNS, clear the client cache or wait out the negative TTL — 'I fixed it but it still fails' is usually this.

example.code:
Resolve-DnsName web01.lab.local -Server dc02
Clear-DnsClientCache
# compare answers per-server to isolate the bad one
example.walkthrough: Break DNS in lab (wrong forwarder); diagnose using the ordered method.

pitfalls: Flushing the server cache for a client problem: match the tool to the layer.
Forgetting negative cache: the fix 'did not work' for 15 more minutes.
Editing the hosts file as a fix: it masks the DNS problem for one machine.
lessons.try_it: Write the DNS triage order into the runbook.

lessons.title: DHCP: Scopes, Options, and DORA
concepts: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. Know it — 'client has APIPA' means DORA failed, and each letter is a diagnostic step (is the Discover leaving? is an Offer returning?).
Scope design: exclusions for statics, reservations for printers/servers (or better: static IPs outside the scope), scope options (003 router, 006 DNS, 015 domain name).
80/20 rule (legacy) vs failover (modern): DHCP failover with load-balance or hot-standby between two servers. No more single DHCP server — a reboot should not stop address assignment.
Lease duration: short (hours) for guest/BYOD churn, longer (days) for stable desktops. Too short = DHCP storm; too long = exhaustion in high-churn environments.

example.code:
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope -ComputerName dhcp01 | Select ScopeId, Name, State
Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 192.168.1.0 | Measure-Object
example.walkthrough: Build a scope with exclusions and a reservation; verify DORA with a packet capture or log.

pitfalls: One DHCP server: its reboot is a network outage for new/renewing clients.
No exclusions for static devices: the DHCP server leases the printer's IP to a laptop.
Scope full with no alert: 'cannot connect' tickets with APIPA addresses.
lessons.try_it: Set scope utilization alerts at 80% and 90%.

lessons.title: DHCP Failover and Troubleshooting
concepts: Failover modes: load balance (both active, split scope) and hot standby (primary serves, secondary waits). Configure via the failover wizard or PowerShell; replicate scopes and settings.
State sync: partners sync lease state; during failover the survivor serves the whole scope. Test it — unplug the primary and watch clients renew.
Troubleshooting: 169.254.x.x = no DHCP response (server down? scope full? relay missing?). Check scope stats, failover state, and DHCP server event log.
Rogue DHCP: an unauthorized server answering Discovers breaks the network subtly (wrong gateway/DNS). DHCP snooping on switches + monitoring for unexpected servers.

example.code:
Get-DhcpServerv4Failover -ComputerName dhcp01
# state should be Normal; test by stopping the primary service
example.walkthrough: Configure failover in lab; kill the primary and verify clients still get addresses.

pitfalls: Failover configured but never tested: the first test is the real outage.
No rogue-DHCP detection: the 'mystery' outage is a home router plugged into the LAN.
Ignoring the DHCP audit log: it records every lease — the timeline lives there.
lessons.try_it: Test failover quarterly; document the result.

lessons.title: DNS Security: Cache Poisoning to DNSSEC
concepts: Threats: cache poisoning (forged responses), tunneling (DNS as exfiltration channel), hijacking (registrar/account compromise). DNS is trusted infrastructure — attack it and everything downstream lies.
Defenses: response rate limiting, disabling recursion for external clients (split-brain: internal vs external views), DNS firewall/RPZ (sinkhole malicious domains), and monitoring query patterns.
DNSSEC: cryptographic validation of DNS data (RRSIG records, chain to root). Protects integrity in transit; does not encrypt queries (that is DoH/DoT). Deploy on authoritative zones you own.
DNS logging: analytical/debug logs show query patterns — tunneling shows as high-volume TXT queries to odd domains. Baseline normal, alert on weird.

example.code:
Get-DnsServerDiagnostics -ComputerName dc01 | Select EnableQueryLogging
# enable analytic query logging to see tunneling patterns
example.walkthrough: Enable DNS query logging in lab; generate tunneling-like traffic and spot it.

pitfalls: Open recursion to the internet: your server becomes an amplification weapon.
DNSSEC 'deployed' but not validated: signing without validation is decoration.
No DNS logs: the tunneling exfiltration is invisible.
lessons.try_it: Decide: split-brain DNS design and whether your zones get DNSSEC.

lessons.title: The Pipeline and Objects
concepts: Everything is an object: cmdlets emit .NET objects with properties, not text. Get-Service returns service OBJECTS — Select-Object, Where-Object, and Format-* shape them without parsing text.
Verb-Noun: Get/ Set/ New/ Remove/ Start/ Stop + noun. Get-Verb lists the vocabulary. If you are grepping text output, you are fighting the shell — filter objects instead.
Pipeline binding: objects flow cmdlet to cmdlet (Get-Service | Stop-Service). ByValue vs ByPropertyName binding decides what connects — check help when a pipeline 'does nothing.'
The triad: Get- (retrieve), Where-Object (filter), Select-Object (shape), then Export-Csv/ConvertTo-Json (deliver). This pattern solves 80% of admin reporting.

example.code: Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running' -and $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic'} | Select-Object Name, Status | Export-Csv .\running.csv -NoTypeInformation
example.walkthrough: List all Automatic-but-stopped services and export to CSV — the classic health report.

pitfalls: Parsing Format-Table output with regex: format cmdlets are for eyes, not pipelines.
ForEach-Object where a direct pipeline works: Get-Service | Stop-Service beats the loop.
Select-Object -First without Sort-Object: 'top 5' of unsorted data is random.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one text-parsing script as pure object pipeline this week.

lessons.title: PowerShell Remoting: One-to-Many Administration
concepts: Remoting runs commands on remote machines via WinRM: Enter-PSSession (interactive), Invoke-Command (fan-out), New-PSSession (persistent). One command, N servers — the end of RDP-everywhere.
Fan-out pattern: Invoke-Command -ComputerName (Get-Content servers.txt) { ... } — parallel by default (throttle with -ThrottleLimit). Collect results as objects with PSComputerName attached.
Sessions persist: New-PSSession once, reuse for many calls, import remote modules with Import-PSSession. Efficient for long admin workflows.
Security: Kerberos in-domain; CredSSP only for double-hop (understand the risk); JEA endpoints constrain what a session can do — least privilege for remote access.

example.code: Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01,srv02,srv03 { Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select CSName, LastBootUpTime }
example.walkthrough: Query last-boot time across lab servers in one command; find the one that rebooted unexpectedly.

pitfalls: RDP to 20 servers for a 30-second check: remoting exists for this.
-ComputerName with 500 hosts and no throttle: you just DoS'd your own admin workstation.
Plaintext passwords in scripts for remoting: use Kerberos/delegation, never embedded creds.
lessons.try_it: Convert your most frequent multi-server RDP check to Invoke-Command.

lessons.title: Scripting: Functions, Modules, and Style
concepts: Functions are the unit: verb-noun names, param() blocks with types, cmdletbinding for -Verbose/-WhatIf support. Scripts grow into functions; functions grow into modules.
Error handling: $ErrorActionPreference, try/catch, -ErrorAction Stop to make non-terminating errors catchable. Decide per script: continue, stop, or log-and-mail?
WhatIf/Confirm: support ShouldProcess in destructive functions (Remove-, Set-). 'It deleted the wrong OU' is not a learning experience you want.
Modules: .psm1 + manifest (.psd1), installed to $env:PSModulePath. Version them. A module is how your team's knowledge becomes reusable instead of tribal.

example.walkthrough: Write a function with ShouldProcess for a destructive op; test with -WhatIf first.

pitfalls: Monolithic 500-line scripts with no functions: untestable, unreadable, undebuggable.
No -WhatIf on destructive functions: the first typo is the last straw.
Copy-paste modules via email: version control exists for this.
lessons.try_it: Turn your three most-used one-liners into a module this month.

lessons.title: Desired State Configuration (DSC)
concepts: DSC declares the desired state (this feature installed, this file present, this service running) and the LCM enforces it — configuration as data, drift as the enemy.
Push vs pull: push (Start-DscConfiguration, ad-hoc) vs pull server (nodes check in, get config, report compliance). Pull scales; push is for lab and bootstrap.
Resources: built-in (WindowsFeature, File, Service, Registry) and community (x*/dsccommunity). Compose configurations from resources; keep them idempotent.

Honest scope: DSC shines for baseline enforcement (features, settings, files). For full fleet config management, teams often pair it with or choose modern tooling — know what DSC does well and where it ends.

example.walkthrough: Write a DSC config enforcing IIS + running service; apply, break it manually, watch it remediate.

pitfalls: DSC for one-off changes: it is a state engine, not a script runner.
Non-idempotent resources: the LCM fights itself every 15 minutes.
No reporting on pull: compliance unknown is compliance unproven.
lessons.try_it: Pick one baseline (e.g., required Windows features) and enforce it via DSC.

lessons.title: Execution Policy and Script Security
concepts: Execution policy is a speed bump, not a security boundary: Restricted/AllSigned/RemoteSigned/Unrestricted control script running, but 'bypass' is one flag away. Real security is AppLocker/WDAC + signing.
Recommendation: RemoteSigned on servers (local scripts run, internet scripts need signature), AllSigned where compliance demands, and sign your own scripts with a code-signing cert.
Signing: Set-AuthenticodeSignature with your cert; verify with Get-AuthenticodeSignature. Signed scripts prove origin and integrity — unsigned scripts prove nothing.
Constrained Language Mode + WDAC is the real lockdown: limits what PowerShell CAN do regardless of policy. Execution policy alone stops accidents, not attackers.

example.code:
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope LocalMachine
Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\Deploy.ps1 | Select Status, SignerCertificate
example.walkthrough: Sign a script with a self-issued code-signing cert; verify the signature.

pitfalls: 'Bypass' in every scheduled task: the policy is now decoration.
AllSigned with no signing pipeline: admins cannot run anything, so they bypass everything.
Believing execution policy stops malware: it never did.
lessons.try_it: Stand up a code-signing cert and sign your admin module.

lessons.title: Hyper-V Virtual Networking
concepts: Three switch types: External (bridged to physical NIC — VM on the LAN), Internal (host+VMs only), Private (VMs only). Choose by isolation need, not habit.
Best practice: separate virtual switches for management, VM traffic, and storage/live-migration. One converged switch for everything is a noisy-neighbor design.
VLAN tagging: Hyper-V supports access/trunk on virtual NICs — the VM's network policy lives in the hypervisor, auditable in one place.
SR-IOV and vRSS: hardware acceleration for network-heavy VMs. Enable where the NIC supports it; measure before and after — acceleration you cannot measure is superstition.

example.code:
New-VMSwitch -Name 'VM-Traffic' -NetAdapterName 'Ethernet1' -AllowManagementOS $false
# dedicated switch, host OS not sharing it
example.walkthrough: Build external/internal/private switches in lab; prove the isolation with pings.

pitfalls: External switch with AllowManagementOS on the only NIC: host and VMs fight for bandwidth.
No VLANs 'because it works flat': flat is not a security architecture.
VMs on the management network: a compromised VM sniffs host management traffic.
lessons.try_it: Diagram your virtual switches with the traffic each carries.

lessons.title: VHDX Storage: Fixed, Dynamic, Differencing
concepts: VHDX (not VHD): 64TB max, 4K alignment, corruption resilience. New VMs get VHDX — VHD is legacy.
Fixed (preallocated, best performance, predictable) vs Dynamic (grows on use, over-provisioning risk — monitor host free space or a growing disk takes down neighbors).
Differencing: child disk records changes over a read-only parent — great for lab/template sprawl, terrible for production (parent loss kills all children, merge pain).
Pass-through and shared VHDX: for guest clustering (shared VHDX) — niche, document why before using. Default to VHDX on CSVs.

example.code:
New-VHD -Path D:\VMs\web01.vhdx -SizeBytes 60GB -Fixed
# fixed for production DB/SQL workloads
example.walkthrough: Create fixed and dynamic VHDX; measure first-write performance difference.

pitfalls: Dynamic disks with no host-space monitoring: the 3 AM 'all VMs paused' page.
Differencing chains in production: backup and merge become nightmares.
VHD for new VMs in 2026: no reason; use VHDX.
lessons.try_it: Set host free-space alerts; document which VMs use dynamic disks.

lessons.title: Checkpoints vs Backups: Know the Difference
concepts: Checkpoints (snapshots): point-in-time differencing disks for CHANGE ROLLBACK (patch testing). They are NOT backups — they live on the same storage as the VM.
Production checkpoints: supported but with I/O cost; never leave them lingering — merged chains grow and hurt performance. Delete after the change window.
Backups: host-level (Windows Server Backup / agent) with application-consistent VSS. That is the recovery story — checkpoints are the undo button.
The classic disaster: 'we have checkpoints' said about a dead host. Checkpoints died with the host. Backups live elsewhere.

example.code:
Checkpoint-VM -Name web01 -SnapshotName 'PrePatch'
# test patch; then: Remove-VMCheckpoint -VMName web01 -Name 'PrePatch'
example.walkthrough: Checkpoint, break the VM, restore the checkpoint, then remove it — full lifecycle.

pitfalls: Checkpoints as backup strategy: they are not; say it in the runbook.
Lingering checkpoints for months: performance degrades mysteriously.
Checkpointing a DC: USN rollback risk — understand it before touching DCs.
lessons.try_it: Audit all VMs for checkpoints older than 7 days; remove or justify.

lessons.title: Hyper-V Replica and Live Migration
concepts: Replica: async VM replication to another host/site (5s/30s/5min intervals) — the poor-man's DR for VMs. RPO in seconds-to-minutes, RTO = failover time.
Planned vs unplanned failover: planned (graceful, zero loss) for maintenance; unplanned for disaster (some loss). TEST BOTH — the button you never pressed will not work when needed.
Live Migration: move running VMs between hosts (shared storage) or with storage (Shared Nothing). Maintenance without downtime — patch hosts on weekdays.
Replica is not backup: it replicates corruption and ransomware too. Replica + real backups = DR; replica alone = a faster way to lose data twice.

example.code:
Enable-VMReplication web01 -ReplicaServerName dr-host -ReplicaServerPort 443
Start-VMFailover -VMName web01   # TEST failover in lab
example.walkthrough: Set up Replica in lab; perform a test failover and measure RTO.

pitfalls: Replica never test-failed-over: the DR plan is a theory.
No backups 'because we have Replica': ransomware thanks you for the second copy.
Live-migrating over a congested NIC: use dedicated migration networks.
lessons.try_it: Schedule quarterly failover tests; record RTO each time.

lessons.title: VM Performance: Right-Sizing and NUMA
concepts: Right-size: start small (2 vCPU, 4GB), measure, grow. Over-provisioned VMs waste host capacity AND can perform worse (CPU scheduling overhead, NUMA spanning).
NUMA: VMs larger than a NUMA node span nodes with remote-memory latency. Keep VMs NUMA-aligned; enable NUMA topology exposure for big VMs.
Dynamic Memory: great for variable workloads, dangerous for SQL/Exchange (use static). Set startup/min/max sensibly — ballooning under pressure is not free.
Measure with the RIGHT counters: Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor, VM Vid Partition, memory pressure — host-level counters, not just guest Task Manager.

example.code:
Get-VM | Select Name, State, CPUUsage, MemoryAssigned
# host view first; guest view second
example.walkthrough: Over-provision a VM deliberately; measure the scheduling cost, then right-size.

pitfalls: 16 vCPUs 'to be safe' on a 2-vCPU workload: slower and wasteful.
Dynamic Memory on SQL Server: performance cliffs under pressure.
Guest-only monitoring: the host tells the truth about contention.
lessons.try_it: Right-size every VM from measured data, not from requests.

lessons.title: NTFS vs Share Permissions: The Two Layers
concepts: Two gates: Share permissions (network entry) and NTFS (filesystem). Effective access = MOST RESTRICTIVE of the two. This single sentence answers half of all 'cannot access share' tickets.
Best practice: Share = Everyone/Authenticated Users Full Control (or Change), enforce the real policy at NTFS. One layer does the work; the other stays out of the way.
NTFS inheritance: permissions flow down; break inheritance deliberately and document why. 'Deny' overrides everything — use sparingly, it creates mysteries.
Special identities: CREATOR OWNER, SYSTEM, Administrators. Know what each grants before touching them — removing SYSTEM breaks backups.

example.code:
icacls D:\Shares\Finance /grant 'Finance-Team:(OI)(CI)M'
# Modify, inherited to files and folders
example.walkthrough: Build a share with open share perms + locked NTFS; prove effective access is NTFS-bound.

pitfalls: Locking down BOTH layers differently: effective access becomes a riddle.
Deny ACEs for routine control: allow-based design is auditable; deny is archaeology.
Removing inherited SYSTEM/Administrators: backups and admin access break silently.
lessons.try_it: Audit one share's effective access with the Effective Access tab; document it.

lessons.title: DFS Namespaces and Replication
concepts: DFS Namespace: \\domain\shares\dept — one UNC path abstracting many servers. Server moves/changes become invisible to users. The namespace IS the interface; servers are implementation.
DFS Replication: multi-master file replication between targets (branch offices, DR). Not for databases or open files — it replicates closed files; conflicts go to ConflictAndDeleted.
Replication gotchas: staging quota sizing (too small = replication stalls), initial sync time on big datasets, and NEVER replicate SYSVOL-adjacent or application databases.
Namespace types: domain-based (AD-integrated, recommended) vs standalone. Domain-based survives server loss; standalone does not.

example.code: New-DfsnRoot -Path '\\lab.local\shares' -TargetPath '\\fs01\shares' -Type DomainV2
example.walkthrough: Build a domain namespace with two folder targets; fail one over and watch clients follow.

pitfalls: UNC paths to \\server\share everywhere: every server migration breaks every shortcut.
DFS-R for SQL databases: corruption — it is not block replication.
Ignoring staging quota: replication silently stops and nobody notices for weeks.
lessons.try_it: Migrate one direct UNC dependency to the DFS namespace this month.

lessons.title: Quotas and FSRM
concepts: FSRM quotas: hard (block) vs soft (warn) on folders — per-user or per-folder. 'The disk is full' should never be a surprise; quotas make it a notification.
File screens: block executables/media in user shares (ransomware and policy). Screens with notifications teach users; silent blocks create tickets.
Reports: FSRM storage reports (large files, duplicates, least-recently-accessed) turn cleanup from archaeology into a scheduled email.
Quota templates: standardize (User Share 10GB soft, Department 500GB hard) — ad-hoc quotas per folder become unmanageable.

example.code:
New-FsrmQuota -Path D:\Shares\Users -Template '10 GB Limit'
# template-based: consistent, auditable
example.walkthrough: Deploy a quota template + file screen blocking executables; test both.

pitfalls: No quotas: one user's video collection takes down the department share.
File screens without exceptions: the dev team's tools get blocked on day one — pilot first.
Quotas set and forgotten: review against growth yearly.
lessons.try_it: Run an FSRM duplicate-files report on your biggest share; act on it.

lessons.title: SMB Security: Versions, Signing, Encryption
concepts: SMB1 is dead: disable it everywhere (it is a ransomware vector — WannaCry). SMB2+ required; SMB3 adds encryption and RDMA.
SMB signing: prevents man-in-the-middle tampering. Required where NTLM relay is a concern — which is everywhere. Enforce via GPO.
SMB encryption (3.x): encrypts data in flight per-share. Use for sensitive shares even on 'trusted' networks — the LAN is not a trust boundary.
Audit: Get-SmbServerConfiguration shows dialect and signing state. Scan the fleet — the 2012 box in the corner is still speaking SMB1.

example.code:
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select EnableSMB1Protocol, EncryptData
example.walkthrough: Disable SMB1 in lab; verify clients still connect (they will, on SMB2+).

pitfalls: SMB1 left on 'for the old printer': segment or replace the printer, not the protocol.
Signing not required: NTLM relay turns your file server into a credential harvester.
Assuming the LAN is safe: encrypt sensitive shares regardless.
lessons.try_it: Scan every server for SMB1; remediate or document exceptions.

lessons.title: Data Deduplication and Storage Efficiency
concepts: Windows deduplication: block-level dedup on volumes (great for VHD libraries, file shares with redundant data — 30-60% savings typical). Not for SQL/Exchange live DBs.
How it works: background optimization jobs chunk, hash, and single-instance blocks. Schedule off-hours; monitor savings with Get-DedupStatus.
Use cases: Hyper-V host volumes (VHDX libraries), user shares, backup targets. Exclude: running VM disks (dedup the host volume, not inside the guest), high-churn databases.
Measure: enable, let jobs run, check savings AND performance impact. Dedup is not free — rehydration costs CPU on read.

example.code:
Enable-DedupVolume -Volume D: -UsageType HyperV
Start-DedupJob -Volume D: -Type Optimization
example.walkthrough: Enable dedup on a lab volume; measure savings after optimization.

pitfalls: Dedup inside the guest AND on the host: double overhead, minimal extra gain.
Dedup on SQL data volumes: latency spikes on rehydration.
Enabling and never checking: the jobs might be failing silently.
lessons.try_it: Evaluate dedup candidates by data redundancy; pilot on one volume.

lessons.title: WSUS Architecture
concepts: WSUS: local update catalog + approvals + reporting. Clients check in, get approved updates per GPO, install on schedule, report status. One download from Microsoft, N deployments internally.
Topology: upstream (Microsoft or parent WSUS) → downstream replicas or autonomous servers. Replicas inherit approvals (central control); autonomous approve locally (branch flexibility).
Products and classifications: sync ONLY what you need (Windows 11, Office — not Itanium drivers from 2009). Every extra product is disk, sync time, and console noise.
Database: WID (built-in) for small, SQL Server for large. Maintain it (reindex, decline superseded) or the console slows to a crawl — WSUS care-and-feeding is real.

example.code:
Get-WsusServer | Select Name, PortNumber
Get-WsusUpdate -Approval Unapproved -Status Needed | Measure-Object
example.walkthrough: Inventory your WSUS: products synced, updates needing approval, client count.

pitfalls: Syncing everything: 1TB of updates nobody needs, syncs that never finish.
WID never maintained: the console takes minutes to open; admins stop using it.
No downstream plan: branch offices pull gigabytes across the WAN per client.
lessons.try_it: Decline superseded updates; run the server cleanup wizard monthly.

lessons.title: Update Rings and GPO Deployment
concepts: Rings: Pilot (IT, fast) → Broad (most users, +7 days) → Critical/Servers (+14 days, maintenance windows). Bad updates hit pilot first, where rollback is cheap.
GPO wiring: separate GPOs per ring (WUfB/WSUS settings: intranet server, install schedule, deadline). Target via OU or group — the ring assignment IS the GPO link.
Deadlines vs schedules: schedule = when offered; deadline = when forced. Deadlines prevent eternal deferral; use them, with user notification configured.
Server patching: maintenance windows + manual approval per server group. Servers do not auto-reboot at 3 AM without a change ticket — ever.

example.code:
# GPO per ring: Pilot-Ring (install Sun 2AM), Broad-Ring (Sun 2AM +7d)
# verify: gpresult on a pilot machine shows the right WSUS GPO
example.walkthrough: Create pilot and broad GPOs; verify ring assignment with gpresult.

pitfalls: One ring for everything: the bad patch hits the CEO and the DC simultaneously.
Auto-reboot on servers: the 3 AM outage with your name on the change.
No deadlines: 'pending reboot' machines accumulate for months.
lessons.try_it: Document ring membership criteria and the promotion timeline.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Windows Update
concepts: Client methodology: (1) GPO applied? (gpresult, registry WUServer) (2) can it reach WSUS? (Test-NetConnection :8530) (3) client state? (wuauclt /reportnow, WindowsUpdate.log / Get-WindowsUpdateLog) (4) CBS corruption? (DISM/SFC).
Common: 0x80072EE2 (timeout — connectivity), 0x8024401C (proxy), updates stuck at 0% (SoftwareDistribution corruption — stop wuauserv, rename folder, restart).
Server side: sync failures (proxy/firewall to Microsoft), approvals not flowing to replicas (check replica config), clients not reporting (check reporting events).
The nuclear option done right: reset Windows Update components via script — documented, reversible, logged. Not 'reinstall Windows.'

example.code:
Get-WindowsUpdateLog
# PowerShell-generated readable log from the ETL traces — read the error codes
example.walkthrough: Break a lab client's WSUS config; diagnose using the 4-step method.

pitfalls: Reinstalling the OS for an update failure: the sledgehammer for a finishing nail.
Deleting SoftwareDistribution as step one: it works, but you learn nothing about the cause.
Ignoring CBS corruption: DISM/SFC exist for the 'updates fail at 98%' case.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-step update triage into the runbook.

lessons.title: Servicing Channels and Lifecycle
concepts: Windows 11/Server: monthly cumulative updates (B release, Patch Tuesday) + annual feature updates. Cumulatives are cumulative — one package brings you current.
Lifecycle: know your build's end-of-service date. Out-of-support builds get NO security updates — the compliance finding writes itself.
Feature update strategy: pilot early, broad within months, never on day one for production. Feature updates are reinstalls — treat them with reinstall-grade caution.
Server: LTSC for infrastructure (long support, slow change), annual channel only where the workload demands it. Servers are not the place for feature churn.

example.code:
# check build and support status
Get-ComputerInfo | Select WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber
example.walkthrough: Audit build versions across the fleet; flag anything near end-of-service.

pitfalls: Mixed unknowable builds: no inventory, no lifecycle plan.
Feature updates via WSUS auto-approved: production gets a reinstall overnight.
Ignoring end-of-service: unpatched CVEs with no fix available.
lessons.try_it: Publish the lifecycle calendar: every build, its end date, the upgrade plan.

lessons.title: Compliance Reporting and Remediation
concepts: WSUS reports: computer status, update status, compliance %. The report is the answer to 'are we patched?' — auditors, CISOs, and insurers all ask.
Target: define compliance (e.g., 95% of clients within 30 days of latest cumulative). Measure it. Trend it. Report it monthly — a number nobody sees is a number nobody fixes.
Remediation workflow: non-compliant list → triage (broken client? offline machine? excluded?) → fix or document exception. Exceptions expire — permanent exceptions are lies.
Stale computers: machines not reporting in 30+ days are either dead (remove) or broken (fix). A WSUS console full of ghosts hides the real compliance number.

example.code: Get-WsusComputer -IncludedInstallationStates Failed, NotInstalled | Select FullDomainName, LastReportedStatusTime
example.walkthrough: Generate the compliance report; triage the top 10 non-compliant machines.

pitfalls: Reporting 'installed' when clients have not reported in months: the number is fiction.
No exception process: every non-compliant machine is 'being worked on' forever.
Ignoring the report: the audit finds what you did not.
lessons.try_it: Publish monthly compliance with trend; review exceptions quarterly.

lessons.title: Event Viewer and Log Strategy
concepts: The three classic logs: Application, System, Security — plus Applications and Services Logs per role (DNS, AD DS, etc.). Know which log answers which question.
Methodology: filter by Event ID and time range FIRST (the log has millions of events; scrolling is not a strategy). Custom Views save your common filters.

Key IDs to memorize: 4624/4625 (logon success/fail), 4672 (special privileges), 7045 (service installed — persistence!), 4697/4698 (scheduled task created), 1102 (audit log cleared — always investigate).
Log size and retention: default logs overwrite — size them for your retention need, forward centrally (Event Forwarding), and alert on 1102 anywhere.

example.code: Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -MaxEvents 20 | Where-Object Id -eq 4625 | Select TimeCreated, @{n='User';e={$_.Properties[5].Value}}
example.walkthrough: Build a Custom View for failed logons; save it as XML for deployment.

pitfalls: Scrolling the log: the event you need is #2,431,007.
Default log sizes in production: the evidence overwrote itself last Tuesday.
No alert on 1102: someone cleared the log and nobody knew.
lessons.try_it: Deploy your top 5 Custom Views to all servers via GPO.

lessons.title: Performance Monitor and Baselines
concepts: Data Collector Sets: capture counters on schedule (daily/weekly), store as blg, analyze offline. This is how 'the server is slow' becomes a graph with a timestamp.
The essential counters: Processor/LogicalDisk/Memory/Network as in systems-anatomy, plus role-specific (AD: NTDS, DNS: DNS, SQL: SQLServer:*). Baseline every role.
Baseline discipline: capture at build, after changes, and quarterly. Store with the server docs. A baseline is the only honest definition of 'normal.'
Alerts: Performance Monitor alerts on thresholds (email, script). Crude but agentless — fine for small fleets; centralize as you grow.

example.code: logman create counter DailyPerf -c '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time' '\Memory\Available MBytes' -si 60 -o D:\PerfLogs\daily.blg -f bincirc -max 500
example.walkthrough: Create a daily collector set; let it run; review the first week's graphs.

pitfalls: No baselines: every performance ticket starts from zero.
Collector sets never reviewed: data nobody reads is disk usage.
Alerting on raw counters without baseline: alert storms from normal variation.
lessons.try_it: Baseline all capstone servers this week; store with docs.

lessons.title: Centralized Monitoring: SCOM, Azure Monitor, and Friends
concepts: Centralize: agents forward metrics/logs to one pane (SCOM on-prem, Azure Monitor/Log Analytics in cloud/hybrid). Distributed logs are unsearchable logs.
What to centralize: security events (4625s, 1102s), service states, disk space, backup results, WSUS compliance, AD replication health. Start with the incident-relevant, expand deliberately.
Alert design: alert on symptoms that need action (disk >90%, service down, replication failing), not on noise. Every alert needs a runbook link — alert without action is spam.
Dashboards: one NOC screen (health by role), one security screen (auth anomalies), one compliance screen (patching, backups). Three screens, not thirty.

example.code:
# Azure Monitor: heartbeat + perf in one query
# Heartbeat | summarize LastBeat=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
example.walkthrough: Design your three dashboards on paper before configuring any tool.

pitfalls: Agent everywhere with no alert tuning: 500 emails/day, all ignored.
Monitoring without runbooks: the alert fires and the on-call googles.
30 dashboards: nobody looks at any of them.
lessons.try_it: Write the alert-to-runbook mapping for your top 10 alerts.

lessons.title: AD and DNS Health Monitoring
concepts: dcdiag: the DC health suite — run it regularly, alert on failures. A DC failing dcdiag is a future outage in progress.
repadmin /showrepl and /replsummary: replication health at a glance. Replication failures are silent until they are catastrophic — monitor them.
DNS: monitor the _msdcs SRV records, forwarder response times, and DNS event log (5501s etc.). DNS degradation is AD degradation.
Automate: scheduled task running dcdiag + repadmin, parsing for FAIL, emailing on trouble. Fifteen minutes to build, catches the 3 AM disasters.

example.code:
dcdiag /test:dns /v
repadmin /replsummary
# both clean = directory healthy; anything else = investigate now
example.walkthrough: Automate weekly dcdiag+repadmin with email-on-failure in lab.

pitfalls: Running dcdiag only during incidents: it is a monitoring tool, not a post-mortem tool.
Ignoring replsummary warnings: 'largest delta' growing means replication is dying.
No DNS monitoring: the first sign of DNS trouble is users calling.
lessons.try_it: Add dcdiag/replsummary/DNS checks to the monitoring baseline.

lessons.title: Alerting Done Right: Signal vs Noise
concepts: Alert principles: actionable (someone can do something), timely (before users notice, not after), and rare enough to respect (alert fatigue kills response).
Tiers: P1 (wake up: DC down, backup failed, disk critical), P2 (business hours: replication warning, WSUS compliance dip), P3 (ticket: informational trends).
Every alert needs: what it means, severity, runbook link, and escalation. An alert missing any of these is a draft, not an alert.
Review monthly: which alerts fired? Which were actioned? Which were noise? Delete or tune the noise — alert hygiene is a recurring task, not a project.

example.code:
# example: disk alert with runbook link in the message
# 'D: below 10% on FS01 — runbook: file-services disk-full procedure'
example.walkthrough: Audit your current alerts against the three principles; kill the noise.

pitfalls: Alerting on everything: the team mutes the channel, then misses the real one.
No severity tiers: the backup warning pages like a DC outage.
Alerts without runbooks: each page is a fresh research project.
lessons.try_it: Run the monthly alert review; publish what changed.

lessons.title: Server Core vs Desktop Experience
concepts: Server Core: no GUI shell, smaller footprint, fewer patches, smaller attack surface. The default for infrastructure roles (DC, DNS, DHCP, file, Hyper-V).
Desktop Experience: full GUI — for RDS session hosts and apps that demand it. Every GUI server is a larger patch and attack surface; justify each one.
Administer Core remotely: RSAT, Windows Admin Center, PowerShell remoting. 'I need the GUI on the server' is a skills gap, not a requirement — close it.
Convert: you can switch Core<->GUI (with a restart, feature dependent). Start Core; add GUI only with a written reason.

example.code:
Install-WindowsFeature Server-Gui-Mgmt-Infra, Server-Gui-Shell -Restart
# GUI install on Core — know it, but prefer staying Core
example.walkthrough: Build your next lab server as Core; do all admin from RSAT.

pitfalls: GUI on every server 'because it is easier': easier to patch, easier to attack, harder to automate.
Core with no remote admin plan: the admin RDPs in and stares at a cmd prompt.
Fear of Core: it is the same OS minus Explorer — the skills transfer.
lessons.try_it: Standardize: Core by default, GUI only with documented justification.

lessons.title: Roles and Features: Installation Patterns
concepts: Install-WindowsFeature is the tool: -Name, -IncludeManagementTools, -Restart as needed. Script every role install — the build is code.
One role per server (mostly): DCs do AD/DNS/DHCP; file servers serve files; Hyper-V hosts host. Combined roles complicate patching, backup, and failure domains.
Feature on Demand: keep the payload available (WIM or FoD) — installs fail without source, especially on Core.
Document the role map: which server does what, why. The next admin (or you in 6 months) should not have to discover it.

example.code:
Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools
Install-WindowsFeature DHCP -IncludeManagementTools
example.walkthrough: Script a full server build: roles, features, baseline config — rerunnable.

pitfalls: Click-through installs with no record: the rebuild is archaeology.
Five roles on one box 'to save VMs': save on licensing clarity, spend on outage blast radius.
No install source: the feature install fails at 2 AM during the incident.
lessons.try_it: Write the role-install script for each server type in the capstone.

lessons.title: NIC Teaming and Network Resilience
concepts: NIC teaming (LBFO): combine NICs for bandwidth and failover. Modes: Switch Independent (no switch config), Static, LACP (needs switch config). Teaming mode: Hyper-V Port, Address Hash, Dynamic.
Design: team the management NICs, team the VM traffic NICs separately, keep storage/migration on dedicated paths. Teams per traffic class, not one mega-team.
Validate: unplug a cable (in lab, disable a NIC) and watch traffic continue. An untested team is a configuration, not resilience.
Modern note: on 2016+, SET (Switch Embedded Teaming) replaces LBFO for Hyper-V hosts — know which your hosts use and why.

example.code: New-NetLbfoTeam -Name MGMT -TeamMembers 'Ethernet','Ethernet 2' -TeamingMode SwitchIndependent -LoadBalancingAlgorithm Dynamic
example.walkthrough: Team two NICs in lab; fail one and measure the blip.

pitfalls: Single NIC on a Hyper-V host: the cable is a single point of failure.
LACP configured host-side but not switch-side: the team half-works and confuses everyone.
Teaming never tested: discover the misconfiguration during the outage.
lessons.try_it: Document teaming mode per host and the test date.

lessons.title: Storage Spaces and Resilient Volumes
concepts: Storage Spaces: pool physical disks, carve virtual disks with resiliency (mirror, parity). Direct: JBOD + software RAID done right.
Tiers: mirror for performance-critical (OS, SQL logs), parity for capacity (file shares, backups). Dual parity for large slow disks (rebuild times).
Columns and interleave: performance tuning knobs — more columns = more parallelism. Default sensibly, tune from measured data.
ReFS vs NTFS: ReFS for virtualization/backup volumes (integrity streams, block cloning); NTFS where features demand it (dedup, quotas nuances). Choose per workload.

example.code: New-StoragePool -FriendlyName LabPool -StorageSubsystemFriendlyName 'Windows Storage*' -PhysicalDisks (Get-PhysicalDisk -CanPool $true)
example.walkthrough: Build a mirrored space in lab; pull a disk (virtual) and watch resiliency work.

pitfalls: Parity for SQL: write penalty hurts; mirror is the answer for transactional workloads.
No hot spare / slow rebuild awareness: the second disk fails during the week-long rebuild.
ReFS where dedup is needed: feature matrix matters — check before formatting.
lessons.try_it: Map each volume to its resiliency level and the reason.

lessons.title: Windows Admin Center and Modern Management
concepts: Windows Admin Center (WAC): browser-based server management — the modern MMC. Gateway model: one WAC server manages the fleet.
Use for: Core servers (GUI-ish without GUI on the box), clustered/hyper-converged management, quick checks without RDP. It complements RSAT and remoting; it does not replace automation.
Security: WAC gateway is a privileged access point — harden it (MFA, limited admins, HTTPS), or it becomes the keys to everything via a web UI.
Automation still wins: WAC for interactive work, PowerShell for repeatable work. If you do it twice in WAC, script it the third time.

example.code:
# WAC gateway install (on a management server, not on every box)
# msiexec /i WindowsAdminCenter.msi /qn /L*v log.txt SME_PORT=443 SSL_CERTIFICATE_OPTION=generate
example.walkthrough: Deploy WAC gateway in lab; manage a Core server through it.

pitfalls: WAC on every server: it is a gateway, not a per-box agent.
WAC as the only admin path: when it is down, have the remoting fallback ready.
Clicking in WAC for fleet changes: script the fleet, click the exception.
lessons.try_it: Define the management stack: WAC for interactive, scripts for repeatable.

lessons.title: Windows Server Backup: The Foundation
concepts: Windows Server Backup (wbadmin): built-in, block-level, VSS-aware. Full server, bare-metal, System State, or volumes — scheduled, to dedicated disk (not a volume with data).
Dedicated target: backups go to their own disk(s), ideally rotated off-site. A backup on the same volume as the data is not a backup.
VSS: application-consistent snapshots (SQL, Exchange, AD aware). Crash-consistent is not enough for databases — verify VSS writers are healthy (vssadmin list writers).
Schedule + verify: daily full or incremental per policy; verify with wbadmin get versions and periodic test restores. An unverified backup is a hope.

example.code:
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C:,D: -allCritical -quiet
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:E:
example.walkthrough: Run a full backup in lab; verify the version catalog lists it.

pitfalls: Backing up to the same disk: the disk dies, the backup dies with it.
VSS writers failed and ignored: the 'backup' is crash-consistent garbage for the DB.
No schedule: the last backup is from the install week.
lessons.try_it: Verify VSS writers healthy before every backup window.

lessons.title: Bare-Metal Recovery
concepts: BMR: restore the entire server (OS, apps, data) to bare metal or a VM from a full-server backup. The 'the building burned' answer for single servers.
Requirements: full server backup with allCritical, bootable recovery media (Windows RE / install media), drivers for the target hardware (dissimilar hardware = driver work).
Practice: BMR to a lab VM yearly. The procedure has sharp edges (disk layout, drivers, boot config) that you discover only by doing it.
BMR vs rebuild: for cattle (DCs, web nodes) rebuild-from-automation is often faster; for pets (the one legacy app) BMR is the plan. Decide per server, in advance.

example.code:
# boot from recovery media -> Troubleshoot -> System Image Recovery
# select the backup version; restore
example.walkthrough: Perform a BMR to a lab VM; time it — that is your RTO.

pitfalls: No recovery media: the backup exists but cannot boot anything.
Never practiced: the driver/disk-layout issues surface during the incident.
BMR as the only plan for DCs: understand USN rollback — DCs have special rules.
lessons.try_it: Create recovery media; store one copy off-site.

lessons.title: AD Forest Recovery Procedure
concepts: Forest recovery is THE disaster procedure: Microsoft publishes the AD Forest Recovery Guide — a 20+ step runbook (isolate, restore forest root, seize roles, clean metadata, rebuild, restore trust). Read it before you need it.
Key decisions: which DC's backup is authoritative (usually the PDC's most recent good one), restore order (forest root first, then children), and NEVER reconnect the failed DCs (wipe and rebuild).
The most common real case is not full forest loss — it is mass object deletion (script gone wrong). AD Recycle Bin + authoritative restore of the OU handles it; know both paths.
Rehearse tabletop-style yearly: walk the team through the guide with your forest's names filled in. The guide is generic; your runbook is specific.

example.code:
# the guide, customized: which DC, which backup, what order
# step 1: isolate surviving DCs; step 2: restore forest-root PDC...
example.walkthrough: Tabletop the forest recovery with your lab forest's actual server names.

pitfalls: Reading the guide for the first time during the disaster: 20 steps under pressure with no customization.
Reconnecting a failed DC 'to help': USN rollback corrupts the directory.
No Recycle Bin: every deletion is a backup-restore event.
lessons.try_it: Customize the forest recovery guide to your environment this quarter.

lessons.title: Backup Testing: Restores Are the Product
concepts: The product is the RESTORE, not the backup. A backup system is verified only by successful restores — everything else is instrumentation.
Test matrix: file restore (weekly, automated), System State restore (quarterly), BMR (yearly), AD object restore (quarterly). Each with a recorded RTO.
Automate what you can: restore a canary file weekly and alert on failure. Manual-only testing decays to never-testing.
Report: backup success %, restore test results, RPO/RTO actuals — monthly to whoever owns the risk. Visibility sustains funding.

example.code:
# weekly canary: restore D:\Canary\ping.txt from latest backup, compare hash
# alert if mismatch or restore fails
example.walkthrough: Build the weekly canary-restore check; let it run a month.

pitfalls: 'Backups are green' with no restore tests: the green light measures the wrong thing.
Testing once at install: configurations drift; the test must be recurring.
No RTO records: the business plans around a number nobody measured.
lessons.try_it: Publish the restore-test calendar; assign owners.

lessons.title: Ransomware Recovery Playbook
concepts: Assume breach posture: backups must be immutable/offline — ransomware encrypts online backups first. Air-gapped or immutable copies are non-negotiable.

Playbook: isolate (pull the network, do not power off — memory forensics), assess scope (which systems, which backups intact), recover (rebuild from known-good media + immutable backups, in priority order), verify (canaries, integrity checks before reconnecting).
Priority order: identity first (AD forest — nothing works without it), then backups/monitoring, then applications by business priority. Write the order NOW.
After: root-cause the entry vector, close it, and run the lessons-learned. The second ransomware event is a process failure, not bad luck.

example.code:
# immutable backup target: WORM storage / offline rotated disks
# verify: attempt to delete a backup as admin — it should fail
example.walkthrough: Verify your backups resist admin deletion (immutability test).

pitfalls: Online-only backups: the ransomware's first target, encrypted with everything else.
Powering off everything immediately: destroys forensic memory evidence.
No priority order: recovery becomes whoever shouts loudest.
lessons.try_it: Write the one-page ransomware playbook; get sign-off on the priority order.

labs.title: Service Triage and NTFS Repair
labs.objective: Diagnose a stopped service via event logs and repair a file-share access problem at the NTFS layer.
steps: Open Services and identify the stopped line-of-business service; note its startup type.
Open Event Viewer and filter the System log for Service Control Manager events around the stop time.
